title: Radiologic Evaluation of the Nasopharynx: A Comprehensive Review.
abstract: The nasopharynx is a critical component of the upper aerodigestive tract and has essential roles in respiration, auditory tube function, and speech resonance. Accurate imaging evaluation of this region allows assessment of deeper structures that cannot be evaluated by clinical examination alone. A thorough understanding of nasopharyngeal anatomy, embryology, and the spectrum of benign and malignant diseases is vital for accurate diagnosis. Key imaging features may be identified across CT and MRI modalities. Although CT effectively delineates local bone and soft-tissue structures, MRI provides superior soft-tissue characterization and allows better assessment of soft-tissue lesions and tumor extension. Disorders affecting the nasopharynx and surrounding structures include eustachian tube dysfunction, cystic lesions, anatomic variations of the clivus, and inflammatory and infectious conditions, as well as neoplasms such as nasopharyngeal carcinoma and lymphoma. Recognizing imaging pearls and pitfalls is useful for accurate diagnosis and to distinguish benign from malignant entities. Optimal patient management-including accurate radiologic diagnosis, early detection of malignancies, differential diagnosis, assessment of disease extent, and posttreatment surveillance-can be achieved through comprehensive radiologic evaluation. © RSNA, 2026 Supplemental material is available for this article.

title: Comprehensive Imaging Review of the Ureter.
abstract: The ureter is an important conduit between the kidney and the bladder and is frequently imaged to rule out cancer in the upper genitourinary tract. However, while malignancy can occur, a spectrum of other pathologic ureteral findings can exist, and these can be divided into congenital, intrinsic, and extrinsic abnormalities that range from postoperative and neoplastic conditions to inflammatory disease. This article provides a comprehensive overview of the ureter, including the ureteral anatomy, ureteral imaging strategies, and various ureteral conditions and their associated imaging features. It is important to identify congenital genitourinary variants, as these are frequently linked to further imaging recommendations, such as nuclear medicine renography and fluoroscopic voiding cystourethrography. Intrinsic abnormalities can be iatrogenic, infectious, inflammatory, or neoplastic. Intrinsic ureteral strictures are most commonly iatrogenic, usually resulting from prior surgery or radiation therapy. Ureteral infections include tuberculosis, schistosomiasis, and Escherichia coli infection, which have varying imaging manifestations. Inflammatory conditions include ureteritis cystica and pseudodiverticulosis. Ureteral masses are rarely benign and are most commonly urothelial carcinomas. Processes in the abdomen and pelvis, including mass effect from pregnancy, ureteral compression from advanced pelvic floor prolapse, and rarely, ureteral obstruction from vaginal devices, also can affect the ureter. The ureter can be injured during pelvic surgery or trauma. It also may be involved by deep pelvic endometriosis, mass effect from extrinsic lesions, or reactive change from inflammatory processes. Radiologists need to have a clear understanding of the patient's history and the range of possible ureteral conditions to establish the optimal differential diagnosis.

title: MR Neurography of Fine-Caliber Nerves: Technical Considerations and Practical Applications.
abstract: MR neurography (MRN) is a powerful tool for evaluating peripheral nerve disorders, traditionally focused on larger nerves like the sciatic nerve, lumbosacral plexus, and brachial plexus. With advances in hardware and software and improved vascular signal suppression, MRN enables reliable assessment of fine-caliber nerves-defined as those with a diameter of up to 6 mm. The small size, variable anatomy, and proximity to vessels and soft-tissue lesions make imaging of such nerves particularly challenging at routine MRI. The authors focus on MRN of fine-caliber nerves throughout the body, offering technical guidance and case-based examples for practical applications. The MRN protocol should include high-resolution two-dimensional and three-dimensional (3D) isotropic acquisitions, with a tailored field of view and appropriate coil selection. Vascular signal suppression is critical and can be achieved using noncontrast or contrast-enhanced techniques, such as postcontrast short τ inversion-recovery (STIR) or steady-state sequences. Sequence optimization, considering parameters like echo time, fat suppression, spatial resolution, and echo train length, is essential to improve nerve conspicuity. A structured approach to imaging and reporting the most clinically relevant fine-caliber peripheral nerves is presented, highlighting protocol suggestions, key anatomic landmarks, and common lesion sites. By applying dedicated imaging protocols with advanced 3D techniques, radiologists can enhance detection of fine-caliber nerve lesions and provide more confident imaging guidance for clinical decision making and treatment planning. © RSNA, 2026 Supplemental material is available for this article.

title: Multimodal Transformer Integrating CT and Pathology for Postoperative Risk Stratification in Stage I Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
abstract: Purpose To develop and evaluate an interpretable, multimodal deep learning model to improve postoperative risk stratification and predict adjuvant therapy benefit in stage I non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Materials and Methods In this multicenter retrospective study of patients with stage I NSCLC, a multimodal model called the Deep Learning-Radiomic-Text Transformer (DLRTransformer) was developed by integrating multiview 2.5-dimensional deep learning features from CT scans, radiomics, clinical variables, and prognostic embeddings extracted from pathology reports using a large language model. A central transformer architecture fuses these features to predict disease-free survival. Model performance was evaluated on independent external datasets and compared with guideline-based risk stratification. Associations between model-derived risk scores and tumor microenvironment features were analyzed to assess biologic interpretability. Results A total of 1073 patients (mean age ± SD, 60.8 years ± 9.8; 550 male) were enrolled from five centers. On external datasets, DLRTransformer demonstrated robust prognostic performance (concordance index, 0.77-0.78), outperforming the guideline-based risk stratification (concordance index, 0.60-0.65). Risk scores were associated with tumor microenvironment phenotypes, including increased neoplastic cellularity and reduced tertiary lymphoid structures. A treatment-by-risk interaction was observed (interaction hazard ratio [HR], 0.14; 95% CI: 0.06, 0.32; P < .01). In propensity score-matched subcohorts, adjuvant therapy improved disease-free survival in high-risk patients (HR, 0.30; 95% CI: 0.11, 0.84; P = .02) but not in low-risk patients (HR, 1.70; 95% CI: 0.97, 2.99; P = .06). Conclusion The DLRTransformer improved postoperative risk stratification compared with guideline-based risk stratification and identified patients with stage I NSCLC who benefited from adjuvant therapy.

title: Management, Upgrade Rates, and Radiologic Surveillance of Screen-Detected High-Risk Breast Lesions.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate the prevalence, upgrade rate, and radiologic surveillance management of high-risk lesions (HRLs) detected at screening mammography in a Dutch breast cancer screening population. Materials and Methods This retrospective analysis of a prospectively maintained database included patients recalled from the Dutch breast cancer screening program between January 2009 and July 2019. Incidence rates, diagnostic work-up, radiologic surveillance, and upgrades to (pre)malignancy after surgical excision and during radiologic surveillance were evaluated. Results Among 17 809 recalled patients, 514 patients with a mean age of 58 years ± 8.1 (SD) were diagnosed with an HRL. The incidence rate of HRLs was 0.83 per 1000 screens and 2.89 per 100 recalls. The majority of HRLs consisted of papillary lesions (34.4% [177 of 514]) and atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) (31.1% [160 of 514]). Surgical excision was performed in 233 cases (45.3%), resulting in 58 HRLs (24.9%) being upgraded to (pre)malignancy. Invasive tumors were mainly found in papillary lesions with atypia and ADH. Of patients diagnosed with an HRL, 324 (63.0%) had an indication for radiologic surveillance. Of these, 257 (79.3%) underwent surveillance, with 109 (42.4%) completing the recommended 5-year surveillance trajectory. During surveillance, 26 patients (10.1%) developed a (pre)malignancy. Invasive tumors were more frequently identified among HRLs upgraded during surveillance than among HRLs upgraded after surgical excision (17 of 26 [65%] vs 16 of 58 [28%]; P = .001). HRLs upgraded to invasive cancer were more likely to be triple-negative compared with screen-detected cancers (9.1% [3 of 33] vs 6.6% [215 of 3277]; P < .001). Conclusion Overall, 16.3% (84 of 514) of screen-detected HRLs were associated with a diagnosis of (pre)malignancy after surgical excision or during radiologic surveillance. Completion of the recommended 5-year surveillance trajectory was achieved in fewer than half of patients undergoing surveillance. Keywords: Breast Mammography, MR-Imaging, Ultrasound, Biopsy/Needle Aspiration, Screening Supplemental material is available for this article. © RSNA, 2026.

title: Risk-adapted MRI Protocols for the Detection of Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer.
abstract: Purpose To compare the diagnostic performance and clinical utility of three MRI protocols for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) according to prebiopsy risk. Materials and Methods This retrospective study included 390 male patients who underwent prostate multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) between January 2019 and April 2024 for suspected csPCa, followed by biopsy. Patients were stratified by Rotterdam Prostate Cancer Risk Calculator score into low-risk (<4%), intermediate-risk (4%-9%), and high-risk (≥10%) groups. Three datasets were generated from each examination: mpMRI (T2-weighted imaging, diffusion-weighted imaging [DWI], and dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging), unenhanced MRI (multiplanar T2-weighted imaging and DWI), and short MRI (axial T2-weighted imaging and DWI). Overall, 1170 datasets were randomly assigned to 10 expert radiologists (117 examinations each). Diagnostic performance for grade group 2 or greater cancer and clinical utility metrics were compared across risk groups. Results Among the 390 patients (median age, 66 years [IQR, 61-71 years]), csPCa prevalence was 34.4% (134 of 390). In low-risk patients, short MRI demonstrated the highest sensitivity (95% [21 of 22]), with no significant differences among protocols (all P ≥ .21) and greatest potential for safe biopsy avoidance (84 biopsies avoided per missed csPCa). In intermediate-risk patients, mpMRI showed higher sensitivity (83% vs 72% for unenhanced MRI and 62% for short MRI; P = .012 for mpMRI vs short MRI) and higher biopsy efficiency (1.11 vs 0.85 for mpMRI vs unenhanced MRI). In high-risk patients, protocol-related differences were minimal (all P ≥ .12). Conclusion mpMRI was associated with improved sensitivity and biopsy efficiency in intermediate-risk patients, whereas protocol differences were limited in low- and high-risk groups; these findings support risk-adapted selection of MRI protocols. Keywords: MR-Dynamic Contrast-enhanced, MR Imaging, Urinary, Prostate, Neoplasms-Primary, Efficacy Studies, Prostatic Neoplasms, MRI, Contrast Medium, Biopsy, Risk Assessment Supplemental material is available for this article. © RSNA, 2026.

title: Causes of False-Negative Screening Digital Breast Tomosynthesis Examinations: A Multireader Study.
abstract: Purpose To classify the causes and pathologic characteristics of false-negative screening digital breast tomosynthesis examinations. Materials and Methods All false-negative screening examinations at a single center from March 1, 2019, through December 31, 2023, were collected. Seven fellowship-trained breast radiologists independently reviewed the false-negative screening and diagnostic mammograms preceding biopsy. For each mammogram, radiologists recorded the cancer as visible or not visible. Cancers were classified as mammographically occult (not visible on mammogram), missed (visible on screening mammogram), or true interval cancers (visible on diagnostic mammogram only). Between-classification comparisons were performed with the Pearson χ 2 test or analysis of variance. Results A total of 117 female patients (median age, 60 years [IQR, 49-70 years]) with false-negative screening mammograms were included. Most cancers manifested symptomatically (88 of 117, 75.2%) a median of 237 days (IQR, 187-301 days) after screening mammography. Among cancers, 47.9% (56 of 117), 26.5% (31 of 117), and 25.6% (30 of 117) were missed, mammographically occult, and true interval cancers, respectively. True interval cancers were more often estrogen receptor- (50.0% [15 of 30] vs 16.1% [five of 31] vs 21.8% [12 of 55]) and progesterone receptor-negative (66.7% [20 of 30] vs 22.6% [seven of 31] vs 35.7% [20 of 56]) than mammographically occult and missed cancers. Mammographically occult cancers were more often stage T0 (32.3% [10 of 31] vs 7.1% [four of 56] vs 10.0% [three of 30]) and detected at MRI (48.4% [15 of 31] vs 3.6% [two of 56] vs 10.0% [three of 30]) and developed in younger female patients (51 vs 62 vs 59 years of age, all P < .05) than missed and true interval cancers. Conclusion Half of false-negative screening mammograms were missed, one-quarter were true interval, and one-quarter were mammographically occult cancer, with differences in pathologic characteristics. Keywords: Mammography, Screening © RSNA, 2026 See also the commentary by Elahi and Slanetz in this issue.

title: Robotic Flexible Ureteroscopy: A Step-by-Step Guide to the ILY® Platform.
abstract: Introduction Robotic flexible ureteroscopy (rfURS) is emerging as an alternative to manual flexible ureteroscopy for the treatment of upper urinary tract stones. Contemporary guidelines and reviews describe its potential ergonomic and radiation-related advantages, as well as comparable surgical outcomes (1-5). Initial clinical and simulation studies with the ILY® platform have demonstrated feasibility, safety, and a short learning curve, although standardized implementation remains limited (6-10). This video presents a step-by-step workflow for the safe and efficient use of the ILY® platform. Materials and methods A 43-year-old woman with a previous right double-J stent placed for obstructive pyelonephritis underwent rfURS for a 13-mm renal pelvic stone (1,497 HU; volume 1,214 mm³). The video demonstrates operating-room setup, robot calibration and sterile draping, robot positioning and fixation, docking to the ureteral access sheath and ureteroscope assembly, console-controlled navigation, laser lithotripsy, systematic renal inspection, and standardized undocking. A flexible suction sheath was used throughout the procedure. Results Draping and docking times were 167 and 645 seconds, respectively. Robotic console time was 115 minutes, including 52 minutes of laser lithotripsy at 8 Hz and 1.2 J. Basket extraction was not required. Undocking was completed in 74 seconds, and total operative time was 130 minutes. No intraoperative complications or troubleshooting events occurred. Postoperative day-1 computed tomography confirmed stone-free status. The patient was discharged at 36 hours postoperatively without complications, as graded by the Clavien-Dindo classification (11). Surgeon satisfaction was rated 8 out of 10. Conclusion rfURS using the ILY® platform was feasible, safe, and effective. A standardized step-by-step workflow may facilitate adoption, improve procedural consistency, and enhance surgeon ergonomics (12). rfURS represents a meaningful step toward autonomous surgery (13).

title: Outcome of Children Treated with Rituximab for Steroid-Resistant Nephrotic Syndrome: Renal Histopathology as a Response Marker.
abstract: Background Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) in children remains a major therapeutic challenge. Although calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs) are commonly used as first-line therapy, a substantial proportion of patients fail to achieve remission, and prolonged use may result in nephrotoxicity. Rituximab has emerged as a potential therapeutic option for refractory SRNS; however, treatment responses appear variable, and the influence of underlying renal histopathology remains incompletely understood. Objectives To evaluate the association between renal histopathological findings and clinical response to rituximab in children with calcineurin inhibitor-resistant steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS). Methods Study Design and Setting:This prospective observational study was conducted between 2011 and 2020 at a university-affiliated tertiary pediatric nephrology center. The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of rituximab in children with calcineurin inhibitor-resistant steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) and to examine the association between renal histopathological findings and treatment response. Twenty-four children aged 2-12 years were enrolled.Follow-up:Patients were followed prospectively after completion of rituximab therapy through regular clinical and laboratory assessments. The mean follow-up duration after the last rituximab infusion was 5.1 years (range: 6 months-8 years).Treatment Response Definitions:Complete remission was defined according to International Pediatric Nephrology Association (IPNA) recommendations as a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) ≤20 mg/mmol (≤0.2 mg/mg) or negative/trace proteinuria on dipstick testing on at least three consecutive occasions.Partial remission was defined as a UPCR >20 mg/mmol but <200 mg/mmol together with serum albumin ≥30 g/L.No response was defined as failure to achieve either complete or partial remission.Genetic Evaluation:Genetic testing was performed in all patients with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), classic minimal change disease (MCD), and MCD with IgM deposition. No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants associated with monogenic steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome were identified in the tested patients. Genetic testing was not performed in patients with IgA nephropathy, membranous nephropathy, C1q nephropathy, or dense deposit disease. Results Twenty-four children with SRNS were included (13 males and 11 females; age range 2-12 years). Histopathological diagnoses included focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) in 9 patients (37.5%), minimal change disease (MCD) in 4 (16.7%), MCD with IgM deposition in 6 (25.0%), dense deposit disease in 2 (8.3%), membranous nephropathy in 1 (4.2%), IgA nephropathy in 1 (4.2%), and C1q nephropathy in 1 (4.2%). Overall, 10 patients (41.7%) achieved complete remission and 3 (12.5%) achieved partial remission, predominantly among patients with MCD and MCD with IgM deposition. Responses were uncommon among patients with FSGS. Eleven patients (45.8%), all of whom were non-responders, progressed to end-stage kidney disease. No major adverse effects of rituximab were observed; mild infusion reactions occurred in three patients and mild cellulitis in one patient. Conclusion In this cohort of children with refractory SRNS, favorable responses to rituximab were observed predominantly among patients with CNI- resistant MCD and MCD with IgM deposition, whereas responses among patients with FSGS were uncommon. These findings suggest that renal histopathology may help identify patients more likely to benefit from rituximab therapy; however, the small sample size, heterogeneous histopathological distribution, and observational study design preclude definitive conclusions. Larger prospective multicenter studies incorporating comprehensive genetic evaluation are required to determine whether histopathology can serve as a reliable predictor of rituximab responsiveness.

title: CVP-BAA: Efficiently Adapting Segment Anything Model for Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Various task-specific medical segmentation models have demonstrated strong performance, their heavy reliance on extensive annotations and highly specialized architectures limits their versatility, scalability, and clinical applicability. Recently, adapting vision foundation models, particularly the segment anything model (SAM), has emerged as a promising alternative. However, prevalent parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) strategies, such as prompt tuning and adapter tuning, often lack an explicit mechanism to embed local structural priors into the long-range dependency modeling of vision transformers (ViT), rendering them insufficiently sensitive to fine-grained details. To address these limitations, we introduce CVP-BAA, a novel hybrid PEFT method that improves SAM's sensitivity to domain-specific textures and local details, leading to superior boundary delineation. The proposed CVP-BAA adopts two key ideas. First, it introduces a convolutional visual prompting (CVP) strategy that leverages convolutional features as structural priors, prepending them to the key and value projections within the multi-head self-attention layers of strategically selected ViT blocks. Through a dedicated prompt generation-and-injection module, this mechanism effectively bridges local spatial details with global context semantics. Second, a boundary-aware adapter (BAA) is designed as a parallel branch to the feed-forward network within the same selected blocks. By explicitly computing and amplifying high-frequency components, the BAA enhances feature representations along tissue boundaries and fine-grained lesion structures. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks across three imaging modalities demonstrate that CVP-BAA achieves superior segmentation performance, surpassing existing task-specific models and PEFT-based SAM adaptations in both quantitative metrics and qualitative results.

title: Lychee: Certified Screening of Inverted Lists for High-Recall Vector Search
abstract: Nearest-neighbor search over embedding vectors matches faces against watchlists, transactions against known fraud patterns, and medical images against confirmed cases, where a missed neighbor is a missed threat, fraud, or diagnosis. Because an approximate index cannot report which queries lost a true neighbor, these applications require recall of 0.999 to 0.9999, at a cost far below that of exact search over billions of vectors. Inverted-file indexes reach high recall by probing more lists, but they read and score every probed vector at full precision, so that throughput falls in inverse proportion to the number of probed lists. Graph indexes saturate below these targets, whereas quantized lists must rerank their candidates with the full vectors. Our insight is to decide for almost every probed vector that it cannot enter the top k of the probed lists without reading the vector, through the certified lower bound of exact search by certified exclusion. This paper turns this insight into Lychee, a GPU inverted-file search that screens the probed lists on tensor cores under a threshold from anchors of the same lists and computes exact distances only for the few survivors. We prove that Lychee returns exactly the k nearest vectors of the probed lists, the answer of an inverted-file search at full precision, while it reads a few hundred full vectors per query regardless of the number of probed lists. On eleven datasets from one million to one billion vectors and against ten GPU and CPU baselines, Lychee is 9.7 to 117 times faster than IVF-Flat at equal recall with 200 probed lists on datasets of up to 100 million vectors. It also reaches recall levels that CAGRA and HNSW do not reach and outruns exact search by certified exclusion by 5 to 18 times above ten million vectors. On four GPUs, Lychee searches one billion vectors at recall 0.9999, 44.5 times faster than IVF-Flat on BIGANN-1B.

title: GWDM: A Guided Wavelet Diffusion Model for Realistic Histopathology Image Generation
abstract: Histopathology images are recognized as a reliable and comprehensive modality for Deep Learning (DL) based diagnosis. However, effectiveness is constrained by limited large-scale annotated datasets, as collecting expert-labeled medical data is costly and time-intensive. Recent advances in generative models, particularly diffusion models, demonstrate strong capabilities in synthesizing medically relevant content for dataset augmentation. Existing generative frameworks treat histopathology patches as generic natural images, failing to enforce biological constraints such as histomorphological structures and heterogeneous staining patterns essential for valid synthesis. We propose a guided wavelet diffusion model (GWDM) framework that captures image details at multiple scales using wavelets and leverages controllable conditioning based on domain-specific histopathological features (e.g., tissue patterns and color variations). We further formulate a histomorphological guidance loss applied to real and generated patches. A loss ramping strategy gradually introduces these constraints during training, ensuring stable optimization and robust modeling of tissue architecture. GWDM was evaluated on three benchmark datasets (BCSS, MoNuSeg, and PAIP2019), consistently outperforming state-of-the-art generative methods. Ablation studies confirmed that domain-guided conditioning, perceptual loss, and structural similarity loss each contribute meaningfully to synthesis quality. Downstream nuclei and tissue segmentation experiments further validated the clinical utility of GWDM-generated images, demonstrating consistent performance improvements when synthetic data augments real training sets. This work shows that domain-specific conditioning and dual-loss optimization generate realistic histopathology patches, reducing data scarcity and improving clinical downstream segmentation performance.

title: H-2DGS: Height-Field Gaussian Splatting for Sharp and Deformable Neurosurgical Surface Reconstruction
abstract: Neurosurgical navigation commonly presents magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as 2D slices, making it difficult to relate the anatomy in those slices to the cortical surface observed through the surgical microscope. We seek a common 3D visualization that combines a photorealistic reconstruction of the exposed cortex during tumor surgery with whole-brain MRI context and diffusion tractography pathways. This requires the reconstructed cortex to form a clear boundary around the brain anatomy rather than a diffuse volume that obscures internal structures. Conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) can reproduce observed views but, under limited surgical view coverage, may distribute opacity through a thick and geometrically ambiguous band. We introduce height-field 2D Gaussian Splatting (H-2DGS), a three-stage pipeline that concentrates a robust 3DGS reconstruction, fuses its depth into a shared truncated signed distance field (TSDF) surface, and represents that surface with curved, surface-oriented Gaussian primitives. Separate height, color, and opacity bases provide local geometry and appearance, while a neighbor-transition objective coordinates overlapping patches. The explicit surface further supports postoperative alignment: MRI-derived depth deforms the reconstruction, and tracked-color supervision with alternating optimization preserves its appearance. Across five real neurosurgical cases, H-2DGS gives low multi-view depth inconsistency, a compact 7.97MB representation, and interactive rendering at 29--42ms per frame. The resulting sharp, deformable surface integrates clearly with tractography and MRI anatomy, including a postoperative resection cavity.

title: Diagnostic Loss: Asymmetric Supervision for Radiology Report Generation
abstract: Automated radiology report generation requires models to do more than produce fluent clinical narratives: they must explicitly state supported diagnoses while avoiding unsupported ones. However, existing medical vision-language models (MedVLMs) are typically trained with token-level maximum likelihood objectives, which prioritize text agreement over diagnostically critical terms. As a result, models can miss key diagnoses and introduce wrong ones. We identify this as an objective misalignment between conventional language modeling and the asymmetric diagnostic requirements of radiology reporting. To encode these requirements, we introduce Diagnostic Loss (DLoss), a differentiable, architecture-agnostic objective that operates directly on decoder token probabilities. DLoss separately aggregates probability mass over vocabularies associated with diagnoses supported by the reference report and with unsupported alternatives. Using asymmetric pooling across token positions in the report, it encourages supported diagnoses to receive sufficient probability in at least one position while suppressing spurious probability spikes for unsupported diagnoses across all positions during training. The loss can be applied to existing 3D MedVLMs without modifying their vision backbones, language decoders, or inference procedures, and introduces no additional inference-time computation. We train and evaluate DLoss on 50,000 abdominal CT scans across several 3D MedVLM architectures on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution report-generation benchmarks. Across these settings, DLoss improves diagnostic faithfulness while maintaining competitive performance on conventional language-generation metrics, showing the value of asymmetric sequence-level supervision for radiology report generation. The code for DLoss is available at https://github.com/gmum/DLoss.

Across these settings, DLoss improves diagnostic faithfulness while maintaining competitive performance on conventional language-generation metrics, showing the value of asymmetric sequence-level supervision for radiology report generation. title: A General-Purpose Dual-Path Interaction Framework for Multi-View Medical Image Segmentation: Alleviating Data Volume Dependency in Small-Sample Regimes
abstract: The performance of medical image segmentation depends on a large amount of annotated data, and most segmentation models experience a significant drop in performance in low-sample-size scenarios. Existing semi-supervised and weakly supervised methods rely on specific network architectures, while traditional multi-view-assisted segmentation methods require strictly paired samples, which limits their clinical applications. To address these issues, we propose DPIF, a general-purpose plug-and-play dual-path interaction framework compatible with arbitrary encoder-decoder segmentation networks, which leverages cross-view anatomical complementarity to reduce annotation reliance. DPIF first performs Sinkhorn optimal transport-based cross-view distribution alignment to establish global semantic correspondence without sample-level pairing. It then adopts conditional mutual information-guided feature decoupling to enable bidirectional knowledge transfer only within the shared semantic space, suppressing view-specific noise. Finally, persistent homology-based topological regularization encodes anatomical invariants as unsupervised priors to mitigate overfitting. Experiments were conducted using 24 baseline models on a private multicenter echocardiography dataset and two public datasets. The results show that DPIF-enhanced models outperform single-view baseline models when trained on comparable amounts of data. Notably, most dual-path variants trained on 40\% - 60\% of the data achieve performance comparable to that of single-view models trained on the full dataset. This demonstrates that DPIF provides a general-purpose and scalable solution for data-scarce multi-view medical image segmentation problems.

title: nnInteractive Agent: General-Purpose AI Agents as 3D Image Annotators
abstract: Interactive 3D segmentation models such as nnInteractive turn a few spatial prompts (points, scribbles, boxes) into accurate volumetric masks, but a human still does the annotation work: finding each structure, placing prompts, checking the result and correcting it. General-purpose AI agents can now interpret images, call tools and write code. We show that such agents can take over this work without additional training: the user makes a request in plain language, and the agent works out what has to be segmented, locates the targets, prompts nnInteractive, inspects the 3D result, corrects it and responds to feedback. Asked for 'the muscles used for chewing', an agent identifies and segments the masseters and pterygoids; asked to count liver lesions, it writes its own code to find candidates and splits a merged lesion on request. Our open-source nninteractive-agent provides nnInteractive as tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), together with a skill that encodes how experienced users prompt it. On a benchmark spanning CT, MRI, PET and micro-CT of humans, a mouse and an ant (14 images; 51 targets from organs and tumours to muscles, foot bones, vessel trees and an insect brain), Claude Code and Codex reach a mean Dice of 0.81 and 0.84 from the request alone; when told where each target is, both reach 0.85 and prompt nearly as effectively as an oracle that places prompts using the reference segmentation. A text-prompted 3D model (VoxTell) is more accurate on most standard radiological targets but less robust: it returns an empty mask for one of them and fails on the leg muscles, the foot bones, the mouse and the ant, where the agents remain accurate. Code: https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/nninteractive-agent

title: Pos4CHD: A Positive-Free Mask-Guided Counterfactual Synthesis Framework for Fetal Congenital Heart Defect Analysis
abstract: The scarcity of positive cases remains a major bottleneck in developing automated diagnostic systems for fetal Congenital Heart Defects~(CHDs), particularly for rare subtypes. Although normal cases are accessible with effort, positive cases are hard to collect due to low incidence rates and privacy concerns, causing severe class imbalance or absence of positive training samples. Existing works resort to synthesizing positives with conditional generative models, but they are task-specific and require positive training samples, hindering application for fetal CHDs. To this end, we propose a positive-free mask-guided counterfactual generation framework for fetal echocardiography, namely Pos4CHD, which enables realistic, high-quality synthesis of pseudo-positive samples from semantic masks, with only normal samples at hand. Technically, we first develop FE-Gen, a mask-guided generative model tailored for fetal heart ultrasound synthesis that mitigates histogram drift and enhances image-mask spatial alignment. Building on FE-Gen, Pos4CHD employs a mask-to-image generation paradigm for CHD synthesis. It first manipulates semantic masks to simulate fetal-heart structural anomalies and then renders anatomically consistent images. Extensive experiments on in-house datasets, together with expert evaluations, demonstrate the visual fidelity~($-12.97$ FID) and anatomical consistency~($+3.96\%$ DSC) of synthesized images. Further validations across diverse real-world CHD diagnosis tasks exhibit promising results and consistent increments, including zero-shot classification~(achieving $93.25\%$ ACC on EbA and $72.92\%$ ACC on TAPVC), lesion detection~($+6.95\%$ mAP50 on VSD), and anatomy segmentation~($+10.49\%$ DSC on fetal heart) compared with baselines. Codes and models are publicly available on \href{https://github.com/DREAMXFAR/Pos4CHD}{GitHub}.

title: A Visual Grounding Benchmark for Retinal OCT with Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can answer clinical questions about medical images, but trustworthy use requires visual grounding: models should localize the pathology they report rather than rely on spurious shortcuts. Whether MLLMs can visually ground clinical findings in retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT), the most widely used imaging modality in ophthalmology, remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce RetinaGroundBench, the first benchmark for biomarker visual grounding in retinal OCT. It comprises 815 B-scans exhaustively annotated by ophthalmologists with 4,537 bounding boxes covering 13 biomarkers across 8 diseases. Because MLLMs often fragment a single lesion into multiple partial predictions, we propose AggIoU, a metric that evaluates whether the union of overlapping predicted boxes covers the annotated region. Across 27 open-source MLLMs (0.8-38B parameters), we find that visual grounding remains largely unsolved: the best general-purpose model achieves a macro F1 of just 23.7%, with consistently low recall, despite reaching up to 73% balanced accuracy on biomarker presence questions. To narrow this gap, we developed RetGrounder, an MLLM fine-tuned using an OCT-specific strategy integrating grounding and textual information. Despite its relatively small size (8B), RetGrounder improves grounding F1 to 33.9%, a 43% relative improvement. Our benchmark provides a reference point for measuring progress in the field of OCT diagnosis with MLLMs.

title: Lightweight Frame Compensation for Real-Time Polyp Segmentation under Frame Skipping
abstract: Real-time polyp segmentation in computer-assisted colonoscopy is hampered by the difficulty of deploying high-accuracy models under strict latency budgets. Frame skipping, which performs inference every K frames and reuses or interpolates the rest, improves throughput but introduces motion blur and lesion misalignment that degrade temporal consistency. To close this gap, we propose the Lightweight Frame Compensator (LFC), a 77K-parameter plug-and-play module inserted before a frozen segmentation backbone. Operating on a three-frame window, LFC fuses consecutive frames via spatio-temporal attention into a single compensated frame, and is trained only on pseudo-labels generated by a differently seeded model, without any expert annotation. Experiments on three polyp video benchmarks show that LFC recovers most of the accuracy degraded by direct frame skipping and, in several settings, reaches the accuracy of frame-by-frame inference, while retaining a 2.05X--2.55X throughput gain. We further evaluate the temporal stability of three backbones spanning CNN, pyramid Transformer, and global-attention Transformer architectures, revealing a spectrum of sensitivity to frame skipping that arises from how locally or globally each architecture aggregates misaligned input. The compensation gain of LFC follows this spectrum: it is largest for high-capacity Transformer backbones, which achieve the best static accuracy but suffer the most under skip-frame inference. LFC thus offers a lightweight, pluggable, and deployment-friendly route to real-time polyp segmentation.

title: Reinforcing intra-operative tumour localisation with weak supervision from pre-operative appearances
abstract: Limited tumour visibility on intra-operative images complicates surgical navigation, including liver hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) targeting on computed tomography (CT) imaging. This makes labelled datasets difficult to curate for deep learning, and transferring pre-operative delineations through registration remains challenging due to intra-operative deformation and lack of paired pre- and intra-operative data. We propose to transfer tumour appearances learned from pre-operative magnetic resonance (MR) images to guide localisation on intra-operative CT through weak supervision. A classifier is trained to classify tumour presence on pre-operative images. This is applied to windows on intra-operative images, and despite the domain gap, it assigns higher tumour-presence probabilities on average to tumour-containing windows. These weak cross-domain signals guide a reinforcement learning agent to localise tumours on intra-operative images. We compare direct transfer, few-shot adaptation and synthetic transfer (trained using unpaired MR and CT), which translates CT into synthetic MR before localisation. On an external HCC cohort, synthetic transfer outperformed other tested methods and CT-only baselines. Our framework enables cross-modality tumour localisation without paired MR-CT training images.

title: The Value of System 1 Models in Medicine
abstract: Many clinical decisions are a choice among a few fixed options, taken quickly and in large numbers. Such decisions also need an uncertainty estimate to know when to defer to a clinician. Generative language models answer slowly in free text and state their confidence poorly. In contrast, System 1 models answer zero-shot with a probability for each answer. However, their performance across clinical tasks is unknown. Four System 1 models, two proprietary and two with open weights, were evaluated zero-shot on 86 public tasks from 14 clinical domains in 20 languages, spanning examination questions and medical imaging. Tasks were assigned to six capability tiers before analysis. The primary outcome was the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUROC). Secondary outcomes included calibration, language effects and comparisons with published results and generative models. Across 179,111 cases, the mean AUROC of the best model per task was 0.94 for medical knowledge, 0.93 for text understanding, 0.83 for clinical judgement from text, 0.89 for image perception, 0.84 for 2D image findings and 0.69 for volumetric findings. Imaging tasks scored 0.09 (95% CI, 0.06 to 0.11) lower than text tasks (P < 0.001). The best model matched or exceeded the best published result on 13 of 26 text tasks and on 8 of 35 imaging tasks. Triage nurses outperformed the best model (accuracy, 0.85 vs. 0.56). One decision took 0.34 to 0.44 seconds and 24 to 81 joules on open-weight models run locally. Accuracy on identical questions fell by up to 39 percentage points from English to Yoruba. Generative models of the same family were 11 to 76 times slower, with 3 to 5 percentage points higher balanced accuracy. System 1 models decide quickly, cheaply and with usable confidence when the answer is stated in a text or recalled from medical knowledge, but not when it must be judged or read from an image.

title: Diffusion-Based Synthesis of Complete 3D Biparametric Prostate MRI
abstract: Synthetic biparametric MRI (bpMRI) may help alleviate the limited availability of large and representative prostate MRI datasets for deep learning applications. In this work, we present a conditional 3D diffusion framework for anatomy-conditioned synthesis of complete prostate bpMRI from anatomical masks. The framework supports sequential synthesis, in which T2w and diffusion modalities are generated by separately trained models, and joint synthesis, in which all bpMRI modalities are generated simultaneously within a single model. Five configurations were trained using PI-CAI, FastMRI Prostate, and PROSTATEx datasets to investigate different conditioning schemes, target modalities, and synthesis strategies. Evaluation using distribution-based metrics, paired-image similarity, and qualitative assessment demonstrated the feasibility of both synthesis pathways. Joint synthesis achieved competitive distributional fidelity while generating complete bpMRI, whereas direct synthesis of ADC and computed high-b-value DWI outperformed their derivation from synthetic diffusion-weighted images.

title: LACToS: Local Anomaly Detection via Conditional Typicality of Superpixels
abstract: Local anomaly detection is the task of identifying spatially confined anomalous or out-of-distribution (OOD) regions within an otherwise in-distribution (ID) image. Most existing methods are designed for a specific context, with a strong focus on industrial defect detection, where they achieve excellent performance on well-established benchmarks. However, we observe that these methods can exhibit significant performance drops in other contexts, especially when the inlier distribution is multimodal. To account for this inlier complexity, we propose LACToS, a principled local OOD detection method based on statistical typicality and made tractable through two innovations: (i) grouping pixels into superpixels and (ii) using a computationally efficient proxy to estimate typicality. We evaluate LACToS across three diverse applications spanning medical imaging, human faces, and X-ray security screening. LACToS performs more robustly than prior methods across these benchmarks. The code is released here: https://github.com/voilalab/LACToS.

title: Predictive Value of the Cincinnati Scale for Code Stroke Activation in Relation to CT Scan Findings
abstract: Background: Stroke is the second leading cause of death worldwide and main cause of disability in adults. Timely care is essential to achieve reperfusion and preserve brain tissue. Efforts have been made to correlate CT signs with the Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale to activate the Comprehensive Stroke Protocol. Analyzing these factors may provide useful parameters for selection. Material and Methods: This analytical, cross-sectional, observational, prospective study was conducted at the Regional General Hospital in Orizaba, Mexico. A total of 497_20 non-contrast cranial CT scans were analyzed using PACS. Patients were followed through medical records until discharge diagnosis was confirmed. Data collection occurred from March 2024_45. Results: 497_2 CT scans were reviewed. The Stroke Code was most often used in the 70-79-year age group, with 56.9% female patients. Of 72_24 ischemic stroke cases, only 24_29 were within the therapeutic window. Conclusion: The Cincinnati scale as a rapid cerebrovascular screen has only moderate to low discriminatory ability. Sensitivity and positive predictive value are very low. Therefore, it is not suitable alone. The results provide opportunity to train doctors to use the Cincinnati scale alongside the NIHSS scale, which has better predictive ability. More public education is recommended to help patients present within the window.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Investigating Pseudo-Learning and Bias Propagation in MRI Brain Tumour Classification
abstract: A brain tumour is an abnormal growth of cells in the brain, which can be either benign (noncancerous) or malignant (cancerous). The 5-year survival rate for benign brain tumours is approximately 85-95%, whereas it is only 35-36% for malignant tumours. Therefore, early detection and diagnosis of brain tumours is important. The recent developments in deep learning have allowed for high precision, accuracy, and automation in detecting these tumours, including both gliomas and pituitary tumours. In this paper, three deep learning-based models for brain tumour categorisation from MRI images are compared to understand the limitations of accuracy-based evaluation with metrics such as class-wise performance and Grad-CAM. To assess the performance and observe various behavioural issues of the models used in this analysis, the MRI scans from the Brain Tumour MRI Dataset from Kaggle and the BRISC 2025 classification dataset containing MRI images from all four major tumour groups were leveraged for their training and testing. The first model serves as a baseline EfficientNet classifier, while the second model applies fine-tuning techniques to improve feature learning. The third model further enhances performance by incorporating multi-dataset training to increase data diversity. The reported confusion matrices show that Model V3 achieved 97.63% accuracy on its 800-image test set. Because its test set differs in size and may differ in composition from those of Models V1 and V2, this result should not be interpreted as a direct like-for-like comparison.The findings highlight the importance of combining conventional performance metrics with Grad-CAM analysis when investigating model behaviour, while further evaluation is needed to establish whether multi-dataset training reduces pseudo-learning or improves generalisation.

title: Predicting high-risk HPV infection and genotype co-infection using genital tract microecological and pathogen characteristics: a machine learning study
abstract: Abstract Background Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) is the principal cause of cervical cancer and its precursor lesions. Vaginal microecological dysbiosis and genital tract co-infections may influence HR-HPV acquisition, clearance, and persistence. However, quantitative prediction models integrating vaginal microecological indicators, genital tract pathogens, and HR-HPV genotype co-infection patterns remain limited. Methods This retrospective study included 3,403 patients who underwent concurrent HPV genotyping, vaginal microecological assessment, and genital tract pathogen testing at the gynecology outpatient clinic of Hainan Women and Children’s Medical Center between January 2022 and December 2025. Of these, 765 were HR-HPV-positive and 2,638 were HR-HPV-negative. Candidate predictors were selected using univariable analysis, multicollinearity assessment based on the variance inflation factor (VIF ≦ 4), and the Boruta algorithm. Seven machine learning models were developed, and their hyperparameters were optimized using grid search with 10-fold cross-validation within the training set. Classifier chains (C ≦ C) and ensemble classifier chains (ECC) were applied to the multi-label prediction of HR-HPV genotypes. Model predictions were interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Results In multivariable logistic regression, Ureaplasma urealyticum (UU; aOR = 2.051), Chlamydia trachomatis (CT;aOR = 1.982), severe bacterial vaginosis score (aOR = 1.614), abnormal vaginal pH (aOR = 1.375), and sialidase positivity (aOR = 1.747) were independently associated with HR-HPV positivity (all P < 0.05). The random forest model achieved the best discrimination in internal validation (AUC = 0.772, sensitivity 0.735, F1 = 0.650). For the ulti-label task, eight HR-HPV genotypes with at least 30 positive cases were included; the ECC model yielded a higher Jaccard score (0.0226) than the independent-label model (0.0190). SHAP identified UU, age, CT, and cocci abundance as leading predictors, whereas a higher Lactobacillus proportion lowered predicted risk. Conclusions Vaginal microecological dysbiosis and genital tract infections were independently associated with HR-HPV positivity. The random forest model showed moderate discrimination, and ECC provided a modest improvement in multi-genotype prediction. These findings may inform risk-based screening, pending external validation.

However, quantitative prediction models integrating vaginal microecological indicators, genital tract pathogens, and HR-HPV genotype co-infection patterns remain limited. Methods This retrospective study included 3,403 patients who underwent concurrent HPV genotyping, vaginal microecological assessment, and genital tract pathogen testing at the gynecology outpatient clinic of Hainan Women and Children’s Medical Center between January 2022 and December 2025. Candidate predictors were selected using univariable analysis, multicollinearity assessment based on the variance inflation factor (VIF ≦ 4), and the Boruta algorithm. Seven machine learning models were developed, and their hyperparameters were optimized using grid search with 10-fold cross-validation within the training set. Classifier chains (C ≦ C) and ensemble classifier chains (ECC) were applied to the multi-label prediction of HR-HPV genotypes. Model predictions were interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). title: Influence of CT Tube Replacement and System Parameter Update on Reconstructed CT Values and Electron Density Conversion Curves in Radiotherapy Treatment Planning Systems
abstract: Abstract Objective Large-aperture positioning CT is a core device for radiotherapy simulation, target delineation, and accurate dose calculation. Replacement of the X‑ray tube, followed by subsequent system parameter updates (including software version upgrade, reconstruction algorithm adjustment, and detector gain calibration), may alter the X-ray energy spectrum and image reconstruction characteristics, thereby inducing systematic drift of CT numbers (Hounsfield Units, HU) and disturbing the accuracy of CT-relative electron density (CT-RED) and CT-mass density (CT-MD) conversion curves in treatment planning systems (TPS). This study aimed to quantify CT number drifts in multiple tissue‑equivalent phantoms before and after tube replacement and system parameter updates using a Philips Big Bore CT 16 scanner, to evaluate the detection efficacy of conventional AAPM TG66 image quality indicators for such occult drift, to reconstruct density conversion curves for Eclipse and Tomo TPS, and to establish a standardized quality control workflow. Methods Fault records and the tube replacement process from August 2023 to January 2024 were analyzed. Tube replacement was performed on January 13, 2024, followed by standard acceptance tests including position calibration, focus correction, long‑tube conditioning, and air scan. System software was upgraded from V3.6 to V4.8 on October 18, 2024, with resetting of reconstruction filter parameters, detector gain coefficients, and air baseline. All CT value measurements, curve reconstructions, and dosimetric verifications were performed after the software upgrade, representing the combined effect of “tube replacement + system parameter update”. Image quality was tested with a Catphan504 phantom according to AAPM TG66. CT value changes in 8 standard materials (air, polystyrene, water, LDPE, PMP, acrylic, Delrin, Teflon) before and after the intervention were compared using paired t‑tests with Bonferroni correction. CT-RED curves (standard and brain‑specific) for Eclipse and a CT-MD curve for Tomo were reconstructed using a CIRS-062M phantom containing 12 tissue‑equivalent materials. Accuracy of the new curves was validated by heterogeneous phantom planar dose verification and real patient plan QA. Results All conventional image quality indicators remained within TG66 tolerances after the intervention. Systematic CT drifts were observed in 7 of the 8 materials except water (P = 0.12, not significant), with drifts ranging 10–30 HU for most materials; Teflon showed a − 63 HU drift (P < 0.001) and air a + 33 HU drift (P < 0.001). Two CT‑RED curves for Eclipse and one CT‑MD curve for Tomo were successfully constructed, all with R² > 0.99. Dosimetric verification showed 3 mm/3% Gamma passing rates for Eclipse ≥ 98.9%, mean point‑dose deviation for Tomo 0.76%, and real patient plan QA passing rates > 98% with no significant differences before vs. after intervention (P > 0.05). Conclusion CT tube replacement and subsequent system parameter updates did not impair conventional TG66 image quality indicators, but induced systematic, material‑dependent CT number drifts that cannot be detected by routine water‑phantom uniformity tests. Re‑measurement of multi‑material CT baselines and mandatory reconstruction of density conversion curves are required. A four‑level quality control process (air calibration, multi‑material CT baseline measurement, curve reconstruction, and dosimetric verification) should be enforced after tube replacement or major software upgrades.

title: Metachronous Bilateral Primary Breast Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma: A Case Report and Literature Review
abstract: Abstract Background: Primary breast lymphoma (PBL) is a rare extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma originating from the breast parenchyma, with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) being the most common histological subtype. Metachronous bilateral involvement is exceedingly uncommon, and standardized treatment guidelines remain lacking. Herein, we report a case of metachronous bilateral primary breast DLBCL with a 15-year disease-free interval and present a comprehensive literature review. Case presentation: A 47-year-old female presented with a palpable left breast mass in February 2026. She had a history of right breast PBL diagnosed in 2011, achieving complete remission after eight cycles of CHOP. Breast ultrasound, mammography, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a BI-RADS category 4B lesion in the left breast. Core needle biopsy confirmed DLBCL with immunohistochemistry demonstrating CD20 positivity (70%–80%), Ki-67 proliferation index of approximately 90%, and negative epithelial markers. Whole-body ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT excluded systemic involvement, confirming the diagnosis of stage IE left breast PBL. The patient received a zuberitamab-containing CMOP (Hi-CMOP). After fivecycles, repeat PET/CT demonstrated complete metabolic response with the Deauville score decreasing from 5 to 1, and breast ultrasound confirmed resolution of the breast lesion. Conclusions: PBL lacks pathognomonic clinical and imaging features, and definitive diagnosis hinges on histopathological examination with immunohistochemistry. For stage IE DLBCL-type PBL, rituximab-based immunochemotherapy followed by consolidative radiotherapy represents a rational therapeutic strategy with favorable short-term outcomes. Long-term surveillance remains essential given the risk of late contralateral recurrence. Multicenter studies with larger cohorts are warranted to establish evidence-based management guidelines.

title: Multimodal Imaging-Assisted Diagnosis of a Rare Primary Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoma Secondary to Imatinib plus Sintilimab in a Postoperative GIST Patient
abstract: Abstract Background: Primary cutaneous T cell lymphoma represents a heterogeneous subgroup of extranodal non‑Hodgkin lymphoma and frequently presents with non‑specific cutaneous manifestations that contribute to high rates of misdiagnosis. Emerging evidence suggests combined treatment with tyrosine‑kinase inhibitors and PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitors may drive secondary lymphomagenesis. This case adds to literature by highlighting the diagnostic value of multimodal non‑invasive skin imaging (dermoscopy plus high‑frequency ultrasound) as ancillary clues before definitive histopathological confirmation. Case Summary: A 58‑year‑old male with completely‑resected high‑risk gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) developed progressive generalized skin lesions following imatinib and single‑dose sintilimab therapy. He presented with widespread purplish‑red scaly papules and plaques accompanied by pruritus, eyebrow loss and palpable peripheral lymphadenopathy. Routine laboratory tests revealed mild monocytosis and slight anaemia. Multimodal imaging including high‑frequency ultrasound and dermoscopy identified characteristic cutaneous changes. Histopathology together with immunohistochemistry confirmed the diagnosis of primary cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma. Unfortunately, the patient was lost to follow‑up after hospital discharge, so post‑discharge therapeutic response could not be evaluated. Conclusion: Multimodal non‑invasive skin imaging assists early suspicion of PCTCL; definitive diagnosis still depends on histopathology and immunohistochemistry. Clinicians should remain alert for secondary cutaneous lymphoproliferative disorders among patients receiving combined targeted‑immune anticancer therapy.

title: A multimodal CT-based machine-learning model for differentiating pulmonary sarcomatoid carcinoma from conventional non-small cell lung cancer: an internally validated study
abstract: Abstract Background: Pulmonary sarcomatoid carcinoma (PSC) is difficult to distinguish from conventional non-small cell lung cancer (c-NSCLC) before pathological diagnosis. We evaluated whether clinical–CT semantic features, radiomics and deep-learning features can support this distinction. Methods: After image quality control, 397 patients (83 PSC, 314 c-NSCLC) from three institutions were analysed. Six models (clinical-only, radiomics-only, deep-only, clinical+radiomics, clinical+deep and full fusion) were developed and evaluated with repeated nested cross-validation (five outer folds repeated 20 times, five inner folds), with preprocessing, feature selection, hyperparameter tuning, classifier selection and threshold selection confined to training folds. Discrimination, calibration and operating-point performance were estimated from patient-level out-of-fold predictions. The influence of CT acquisition heterogeneity was examined in sensitivity analyses. Results: The prespecified full fusion model achieved an AUROC of 0.890 (95% CI 0.848–0.930) and an AUPRC of 0.739 (0.643–0.823; PSC prevalence 0.209). At a training-derived high-sensitivity threshold, sensitivity and specificity were 0.855 and 0.755. The clinical+radiomics model performed similarly (AUROC 0.895, 0.851–0.934), the clinical-only model reached 0.843 (0.796–0.887), and deep features alone were not discriminative (AUROC 0.533). Intratumoral low-attenuation area (LAA) presence and LAA ratio were independently associated with PSC. Acquisition parameters alone also discriminated the groups (AUROC 0.901); after adjustment for acquisition variables, radiomics retained incremental value over clinical features (ΔAUROC 0.075, P<0.001), but residual confounding by source or protocol cannot be excluded. Conclusions: Intratumoral LAA features and CT radiomics may help flag PSC before pathology in an internally validated setting, whereas Kinetics-pretrained deep features added no value. Because acquisition heterogeneity may contribute to imaging-based performance and a negative prediction cannot exclude PSC, the model should be regarded as exploratory and requires external validation with standardized acquisition before clinical use.

title: Translating Imaging-based Brain Age Models for Predicting Accelerated Brain Ageing in African Populations: A Pilot Study on a Nigerian Cohort.
abstract: Abstract Background: Brain age is an emerging imaging biomarker for early detection of neurodegenerative disorders, based on the estimation of the brain’s biological age. Existing predictive models are predominantly trained on Global North (GN) neuroimaging data, limiting their sensitivity when applied to underrepresented populations due to geographic, imaging scanner, and biological heterogeneity. We investigated this bias by adapting the standard Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) method to a population-specific (PS) brain age model. Methods: Using a multi-institutional T1-weighted brain MRI dataset from 309 Nigerian adults, we implemented a robust low-compute image analysis pipeline which includes repurposing clinical scans and high-resolution cortical parcellation with multi-stage quality control. The PS-GPR model was trained on regional brain volumetric features from the Nigerian MRI scans and its performance compared to four common GN pre-trained models. Results: The proposed PS-GPR model showed a significantly lower prediction error (mean absolute error = 9.82 years) without age-bias correction and few seconds inference time compared to GN-trained machine learning models (mean absolute error = 10.00 – 16.70 years). SPARROW, a generalizable deep learning framework achieved an MAE of 7.87 but failed on 6% of the test set. This early work demonstrates the importance of representative data to build resource-efficient clinically viable models. Conclusion: This population-specific model is a step towards sensitive low-compute African brain age models. With the expansion of imaging data beyond Nigeria through the Africa Neuroimaging Archive (AfNiA), we will further develop the PS model to identify individuals with accelerated brain ageing for early intervention in at-risk adults.

title: Multifocal Well-Differentiated Small Intestinal Neuroendocrine Tumor Presenting as Partial Small Bowel Obstruction in an Elderly Female: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background Small intestinal neuroendocrine tumors (SI-NETs) are rare, slow-growing malignancies that frequently present with nonspecific gastrointestinal symptoms, leading to diagnostic delays averaging five to seven years. Despite the existence of blood-based biomarkers including serum chromogranin A and urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), most patients continue to present with advanced locoregional or metastatic disease. This case illustrates the diagnostic and surgical challenges of SI-NET in an elderly patient and highlights the clinical consequences of delayed biomarker utilization. Case presentation: A 77-year-old White female was referred to a surgical clinic after her primary care physician identified a small bowel mass on imaging ordered for chronic abdominal discomfort and a 20-pound unintentional weight loss. CT imaging demonstrated a solid mesenteric mass with adjacent adenopathy and small bowel tethering, producing the characteristic spoke-wheel sign of mesenteric desmoplasia. Serum chromogranin A and urinary 5-HIAA were not obtained prior to surgical referral. She underwent exploratory laparotomy with open small bowel resection and side-to-side anastomosis. Surgical pathology confirmed multifocal, well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor (Grade 1, Ki-67 ~ 1%), staged pT4N1, with lymphovascular and perineural invasion and a positive mesenteric margin. Postoperative Dotatate PET identified a single PET-avid mesenteric lesion, prompting referral to a tertiary hepatobiliary center. A second exploratory laparotomy resected a 1.5 cm mesenteric nodule requiring direct repair of a superior mesenteric artery branch. Final pathology demonstrated fibrosis and chronic inflammation with no residual neuroendocrine tumor. The patient elected active surveillance with annual follow-up. Conclusions This case demonstrates the striking discordance between low tumor grade and advanced locoregional disease extent in SI-NETs and underscores the missed opportunity for earlier detection through routine biomarker screening in symptomatic patients. The PET-positive mesenteric nodule that yielded only fibrosis on re-resection raises important questions about functional imaging specificity in the desmoplastic postoperative mesentery. Clinicians should maintain a low threshold for obtaining serum chromogranin A and urinary 5-HIAA in patients presenting with unexplained weight loss and chronic gastrointestinal symptoms.

title: FLNA-related periventricular nodular heterotopia with multisystem involvement: a case report
abstract: Abstract Background FLNA-related periventricular nodular heterotopia (PVNH) is an X-linked neuronal migration disorder classically associated with epilepsy. Accumulating evidence indicates that it is a multisystem disorder involving cardiac valvular, pulmonary, and ophthalmologic manifestations. We report a patient with an unusually comprehensive multisystem phenotype to emphasize the need for systematic extracranial evaluation in FLNA-related PVNH. Case presentation: A 33-year-old woman presented with two decades of headache and palpitations. Physical examination revealed digital clubbing and prominently dilated cardiac valves. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral periventricular heterotopia. Enhanced whole-exome sequencing identified a heterozygous pathogenic nonsense variant in FLNA (NM_001110556.2:c.2193C > G, p.Tyr731Ter). Multisystem involvement comprised focal epilepsy, polyvalvular regurgitation, interstitial lung disease, and ophthalmologic abnormalities. Seizures were controlled with oxcarbazepine and lamotrigine, and the patient was referred for coordinated cardiologic, pulmonary, and ophthalmologic follow-up. Conclusions FLNA-related PVNH should be managed as a multisystem disorder rather than isolated epilepsy. Routine cardiovascular, pulmonary, and ophthalmologic screening, combined with genetic counseling for X-linked dominant transmission, should be integrated into standard care.

title: Preoperative diffusion-perivascular MRI burden and postoperative delirium after subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation in Parkinson disease
abstract: Abstract Postoperative delirium after subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation may reflect pre-existing brain vulnerability, but the preoperative imaging correlates of this vulnerability remain uncertain. We examined whether a combined diffusion and perivascular imaging burden was associated with delirium after bilateral subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation. This single-centre observational cohort included 100 patients with Parkinson disease undergoing bilateral subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation and 32 healthy controls scanned with the same preoperative MRI protocol. Delirium was assessed during postoperative days using the Nursing Delirium Screening Scale with clinical adjudication. Age- and sex-adjusted reference models fitted in healthy controls were used to standardise tract diffusion metrics, diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space, and basal ganglia enlarged perivascular space counts. Directionally aligned diffusion and perivascular scores were averaged with equal domain weights. Patients who developed postoperative delirium (n = 30) had higher combined burden than those who did not (n = 70; 95% CI, 0.584 to 1.526; q<.001). Using Firth penalised logistic regression, higher combined burden remained associated with postoperative delirium after adjustment for age, sex, education, Mini-Mental State Examination score, disease duration, and motor severity (95% CI, 1.49 to 4.25; Wald P<.001). Higher burden was also associated with longer delirium duration and higher peak screening scores among affected patients. Exploratory internal prediction yielded an area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve of 0.701 after adding burden to clinical variables, compared with 0.538 for clinical variables alone. These findings support preoperative diffusion-perivascular burden as a candidate marker of perioperative neuropsychiatric vulnerability requiring multicentre validation.

Using Firth penalised logistic regression, higher combined burden remained associated with postoperative delirium after adjustment for age, sex, education, Mini-Mental State Examination score, disease duration, and motor severity (95% CI, 1.49 to 4.25; Wald P<.001). Higher burden was also associated with longer delirium duration and higher peak screening scores among affected patients. Exploratory internal prediction yielded an area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve of 0.701 after adding burden to clinical variables, compared with 0.538 for clinical variables alone. These findings support preoperative diffusion-perivascular burden as a candidate marker of perioperative neuropsychiatric vulnerability requiring multicentre validation.

title: Germline Whole-Gene Deletion of SDHA in a Carotid Body Paraganglioma Identified by Whole-Genome Sequencing and Confirmed by MLPA: A Case Report and Review of the Literature
abstract: Abstract Background : Carotid body paragangliomas are frequently associated with germline variants in succinate dehydrogenase ( SDH ) genes. Among these, SDHA variants are particularly challenging to diagnose due to low penetrance and the presence of highly homologous pseudogenes. Standard diagnostic workflows, including whole-exome sequencing and targeted panels, often fail to detect large structural variants, such as whole-gene deletions, leading to potential underdiagnosis. This case is the first to report a germline whole-gene deletion of SDHA identified via whole-genome sequencing (WGS), providing definitive physical evidence of the Knudson two-hit hypothesis through the somatic loss of the remaining allele in the tumor tissue. Case presentation : A 63-year-old female presented with a 2-cm, left carotid body tumor. There was no relevant family history. The tumor was successfully resected, and histopathology confirmed a paraganglioma. While immunohistochemistry showed a loss of both SDHA and SDHB expression, WGS of peripheral blood revealed what is, to our knowledge, the first reported germline whole-gene deletion of the SDHA gene (copy number ≈ 1.1) in the region chr5:210,651–314,171. Notably, this type of large structural variant is potentially elusive to standard genetic analysis workflows. Subsequent WGS of the tumor tissue confirmed biallelic inactivation through the loss of the remaining allele (copy number ≈ 0.86), representing a classic two-hit mechanism. This large-scale deletion of all SDHA exons was further validated using multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA), confirming it as the pathogenic driver. The patient remains under rigorous long-term follow-up given the reported 15% risk of malignancy associated with SDHA variants. Conclusions : This case highlights the clinical utility of WGS in overcoming the inherent limitations of exome-based sequencing for SDHA analysis. When clinical suspicion remains high - specifically in cases with SDHA-negative immunohistochemistry but negative standard genetic testing - WGS or MLPA should be employed to detect hidden structural variants. Accurate molecular diagnosis is essential not only for understanding the mechanism of tumorigenesis but also for tailoring oncological surveillance and genetic counseling for the patient and their family.

title: Operator-rated puncture performance and first-pass lesion tissue area in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: an exploratory single-center sub-analysis of endoscopic ultrasound- guided tissue acquisition
abstract: Abstract Background: Adequate tissue acquisition is important for histological assessment and ancillary testing in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). We primarily explored the association between operator-rated puncture performance and first-pass lesion tissue area during endoscopic ultrasound-guided tissue acquisition (EUS-TA) in patients with PDAC. A secondary analysis examined whether this association was observed in the overall cohort, irrespective of final diagnosis. Methods: This exploratory single-center sub-analysis used prospective data from a multicenter randomized trial of 22-gauge fine-needle biopsy needles. Endoscopists rated overall puncture performance on a five-point scale after EUS-TA. Ratings were analyzed using two post hoc dichotomizations: very easy/easy versus indeterminate/difficult/very difficult, and very easy versus all other ratings. First-pass lesion tissue area was quantified automatically on histological slides using a digital microscope with image-analysis software. Multivariable linear regression assessed associations between ratings and tissue areas in each cohort, adjusting for needle type, puncture route, operator experience, and lesion size. Firth logistic regression assessed associations between ratings and exploratory ≥ 4-mm² benchmark attainment in the PDAC cohort. Trends in tissue area across very easy, easy, and remaining ratings were assessed using the Jonckheere–Terpstra test. Comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) suitability was summarized descriptively. Results: Of 62 patients, 48 had PDAC. In the PDAC cohort, the very easy/easy comparison yielded inconclusive adjusted associations with tissue area and benchmark attainment. A very easy rating was associated with greater tissue area (median, 5.45 vs. 1.90 mm²; adjusted difference, 1.93 mm²; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.12–3.74) and benchmark attainment (57.7% vs. 22.7%; adjusted odds ratio, 4.44; 95% CI, 1.17–21.06). Tissue area decreased with less favorable ratings (p for trend = 0.016). Two of six patients assessed for CGP were considered suitable. In the overall cohort, lesion size remained associated with tissue area, whereas adjusted associations for both rating dichotomizations were inconclusive. Tissue area decreased with less favorable ratings (p for trend = 0.034). Conclusions: In patients with PDAC, an endoscopist’s very easy rating was associated with greater first-pass lesion tissue area after adjustment for lesion size and procedural factors. Prospective pass-by-pass studies are needed to validate this exploratory association and determine its utility in EUS-TA. Trial registration: Parent trial: Japan Registry of Clinical Trials (jRCT), jRCT1042220099, registered on 25 November 2022.

title: Central nervous system aspergillosis with negative serum fungal biomarkers after sequential teclistamab and talquetamab for multiple myeloma: a case report and review of the literature
abstract: Abstract Bispecific antibodies directed against B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) and G protein-coupled receptor class C group 5 member D (GPRC5D) have improved outcomes in relapsed multiple myeloma but are associated with a high burden of infection. Invasive mould infection of the central nervous system (CNS) has rarely been described in this setting. We report a 70-year-old woman with heavily pretreated IgG-kappa myeloma who received teclistamab, complicated by immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) treated with corticosteroids, followed by talquetamab. She received antiviral and anti- Pneumocystis prophylaxis and intravenous immunoglobulin, without mould-active cover. Shortly after starting talquetamab, she developed cough and confusion, with cavitating pulmonary lesions initially attributed to bacterial abscesses. Serum galactomannan remained 0.1 on serial testing and β-D-glucan was negative. Computed tomography-guided lung biopsy confirmed pulmonary aspergillosis, and voriconazole was started. Failure to regain her functional baseline and progressive weakness, initially difficult to separate from her previous ICANS, led to brain magnetic resonance imaging, which showed a 10-mm ring-enhancing occipital lesion. Biopsy confirmed CNS aspergillosis. A literature review identified few published cases of invasive aspergillosis during bispecific therapy for myeloma, and serum galactomannan was positive in those with reported results. Negative fungal biomarkers should not exclude invasive aspergillosis in patients receiving bispecific antibodies, and new neurological decline warrants imaging and tissue diagnosis even after ICANS. Patients who require corticosteroids for ICANS during bispecific therapy, particularly after sequential bispecific exposure, may warrant individualised assessment of invasive mould risk and consideration of azole prophylaxis, pending prospective evaluation.
