title: Post-registration medical imaging education as a pathway to addressing the specialist deficit in Rwanda: A needs assessment.
abstract: Introduction Sub-Saharan Africa faces a critical shortage of specialist medical imaging practitioners, yet undergraduate training remains insufficient for advanced practice. Rwanda's "4 × 4 Reform" prioritises expanding the radiology workforce, but evidence-based curriculum development for postgraduate education remains lacking. This study aimed to conduct a multi-stakeholder needs assessment to inform the design, structure, and delivery of a proposed Master of Science in Medical Imaging at the University of Rwanda, College of Medicine and Health Sciences. Methods An online cross-sectional survey was conducted nationally, recruiting 210 participants from multiple stakeholder groups, including clinical practitioners, educators, policymakers, and patient representatives. Data were analysed with descriptive statistics and Fisher's exact tests in R. Results Advanced image interpretation skills were identified as hugely lacking by 72.9% of respondents. Diagnostic ultrasound (68.8%), pattern recognition (65.2%), computed tomography (61.7%), and magnetic resonance imaging (60.7%) were the top priorities. Notably, 79.0% (n = 166) of stakeholders expected graduates to develop leadership and management skills, followed by teaching and curriculum development (73.8%). Fisher's exact tests comparing clinical practitioners (n = 142) with other stakeholders (n = 68) found no significant differences across all seven skills assessed (ultrasound: p = 0.2; pattern recognition: p = 0.2; CT: p = 0.4; MRI: p = 0.5; radiography: p > 0.9; nuclear medicine: p = 0.9; radiation therapy: p = 0.6). Conclusions This empirical assessment in Rwanda reveals an urgent need for specialist training that integrates advanced clinical competencies with leadership and education skills. Implications for practice This study offers a guide for integrating advanced clinical skills with leadership and educational competencies into postgraduate curricula, directly addressing critical workforce shortages in low-resource settings.

title: Advancing nanomaterials for treatment of eye diseases: a review.
abstract: Ocular diseases involving both the anterior and posterior segments-such as dry eye disease, keratitis, glaucoma, cataracts, diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion, and ocular tumors-remain major contributors to global visual impairment. Conventional topical and systemic therapies are limited by rapid clearance, restricted penetration across ocular barriers, and poor bioavailability, particularly for posterior-segment targets. Nanotechnology has introduced a transformative therapeutic paradigm by enabling controlled pharmacokinetics, enhanced tissue penetration, and site-specific delivery. A wide range of engineered nanomaterials-including polymeric nanoparticles, lipid-based carriers, dendrimers, metallic and metal-oxide nanoparticles, mesoporous silica systems, cerium oxide nanozymes, carbon quantum dots, nanogels, and electrospun nanofibers-has demonstrated improved drug loading, sustained release, ocular surface retention, and compatibility with biologics and gene-based agents. Emerging minimally invasive platforms, such as 4D printed smart scaffolds, dissolving microneedles and magnetically driven microrobots, further enable precise transscleral or intravitreal delivery, active navigation through the vitreous, and targeted interaction with retinal lesions. Parallel clinical advances, including FDA-approved nanoformulations and ongoing trials, confirm the translational potential of these technologies. Plus, artificial intelligence now accelerates both ophthalmic diagnosis and nanocarrier design, enabling predictive modeling of nano-bio interactions, personalized delivery strategies, and real-time disease assessment. This review integrates current advances in nanomaterial engineering and AI-guided innovation, outlining their convergent roles in shaping next-generation precision therapeutics for vision preservation and restoration.

title: Impact of Photon-Counting CT Acquisition Modes on Coronary Stenosis Assessment and Radiation Dose: A Phantom and Clinical Evaluation.
abstract: Introduction Photon-counting detector computed tomography (PCD-CT) offers high spatial resolution and dose-efficient coronary CT angiography (cCTA), but protocol selection, especially optimal acquisition mode, requires balancing spacial resolution, temporal robustness and radiation exposure. This study evaluated various PCD-CT acquisition modes in terms of image quality, blooming, stenosis grading, diagnostic accuracy, and radiation dose using phantom and clinical cCTA. Methods First-generation dual-source PCD-CT was used with four acquisition modes: high-pitch spiral with prospective ECG-gating (Flash), Sequence, Spiral, and retrospective ultra-high-resolution (UHR) spiral mode. Phantom experiments used six 3D-printed coronary artery models with stenoses ranging from 21% to 73%. In a retrospective clinical study, 41 cCTA examinations were analyzed. Qualitative and quantitative image assessments used invasive coronary angiography as reference standard for diagnostic accuracy. Patient characteristics and radiation doses were recorded. Results UHR demonstrated the highest image quality and the lowest quantitative blooming in phantom and clinical data (clinical image quality score: UHR 4.12 ± 0.99 vs. Flash 3.00 ± 0.86; p = 0.002). Diagnostic accuracy varied across protocols for detecting ≥50% and ≥70% stenoses was high across all modes (e.g., Flash: 76.5% each; Sequence: 100% and 57.1%; UHR: 64.7% and 82.4%). Radiation dose was highest in UHR (26.44 ± 9.76 mSv) compared with Sequence (13.65 ± 8.86 mSv) and Flash (1.40 ± 0.32 mSv); all p ≤ 0.011. Conclusion While UHR acquisition provides highest image quality in PCD-CT cCTA, lower-dose acquisition modes achieve comparable diagnostic accuracy for coronary stenosis detection. Protocol selection should therefore be individualized, and prospective controlled studies are required.

title: Uterine leiomyomas in HLRCC: a scoping review of presentation, histopathology, treatment patterns, and reproductive implications.
abstract: Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC) is a rare cancer predisposition syndrome in which uterine leiomyomas (ULs) are common, morbid, and often precede renal cancer diagnosis. We synthetized evidence on the clinical presentation, pathology, management, and reproductive outcomes of HLRCC-associated ULs. MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched for peer-reviewed studies reporting original data on ULs in HLRCC. Two reviewers independently screened articles and extracted data. Individual patient data from 410 patients and aggregate data from 27 observational studies were included. Mean age at UL diagnosis was 32.4 years. Most patients (89.1%) had multiple fibroids, were symptomatic (88.1%), and commonly reported abnormal uterine bleeding (80.6%) or pelvic pain (41.2%). Average maximum fibroid size was 7.5 cm. Fumarate hydratase (FH) and/or S-(2-succino)cysteine (2SC) immunohistochemistry studies showed abnormal staining in >85% of tumors. Surgical intervention was required in 94.4% of patients; hysterectomy was most common (67.0%), at a mean age of 35.2 years, whereas myomectomy was performed in 27% at 27.7 years. Despite a family history of HLRCC-related features in 88.8% of patients, only 0.6% underwent germline FH testing before gynecologic diagnosis. Fertility and obstetric outcomes were sparsely reported. Uterine leiomyosarcoma was rare, with an uncertain syndromic association. HLRCC-associated ULs are genetically, morphologically, and clinically distinct from sporadic fibroids, yet remain under-recognized. Integrating age, multiplicity, symptoms, family history, and pathology-triggered FH/2SC immunohistochemistry into gynecologic practice would enable earlier germline testing, renal surveillance, and reproductive counseling. Prospective registries are needed to define genotype-phenotype relationships, fertility outcomes, and leiomyosarcoma risk.

title: The β-cells in type 1 diabetes mellitus: findings from human pancreas studies.
abstract: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by long-term and dynamic interactions between the immune system and pancreatic β-cells, ultimately leading to severe insulin deficiency. A paradigm shift in T1DM research has occurred in the past few years, with research now focusing on the human disease because of access to human pancreatic tissue and pancreas-draining lymph nodes. Advances in high-resolution imaging, single-cell and spatial multi-omics, and histopathology based on artificial intelligence have profoundly reshaped our understanding of disease initiation and progression. These studies revealed that β-cell loss and/or dysfunction might begin earlier than previously appreciated, preferentially affecting small β-cell-rich islets and insulin-positive cell clusters, with larger islets showing transient resistance. Substantial β-cell mass often persists at diagnosis, accompanied by functional impairment rather than immediate cell death. Across disease stages, β-cells exhibit conserved molecular signatures dominated by interferon signalling, enhanced antigen presentation and adaptive immune-evasion programmes, with evidence of heterogeneity linked to age, disease duration and immune context. Parallel analyses of pancreatic lymph nodes show early immune dysregulation, including altered regulatory T cell signatures and expansion of stem-like cytotoxic T cell populations, even before overt hyperglycaemia. Together, these findings support an integrated model of T1DM progression that enables alignment of clinical staging with evolving β-cell and immune phenotypes.

title: Thermosensitive RGD-modified liposomes co-loading Fe<sub>3</sub>O<sub>4</sub> and sorafenib for synergistic photothermal-chemotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Sorafenib (SRF) therapy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is limited by dose-limiting toxicities, inadequate tumor exposure, and the inability to confine drug action spatiotemporally, leading to suboptimal efficacy and a narrow therapeutic window. Here we report an RGD-functionalized DPPC-based thermosensitive liposomal theranostic system co-encapsulating Fe 3 O 4 nanoparticles and SRF (RGD-Fe 3 O 4 /SRF@TSL) to enable MRI-guided window selection and near-infrared (NIR)-triggered, on-demand chemotherapy potentiation. The nanosystem is colloidally stable (208 nm) and exhibits a phase transition at 41 °C. Accordingly, SRF release is sharply temperature-gated, reaching 88% at 45 °C but only 26% at 37 °C within 18 h (3.4-fold enhancement). Fe 3 O 4 confers strong T 2 MRI contrast ( r 2 = 136.4 mM -1 s -1 ) and photothermal conversion ( η = 24.73%), enabling noninvasive tracking of tumor accumulation and controllable local heating that elevates tumor-surface temperature to 56 °C within 5 min under 808 nm irradiation. Dynamic MRI identifies a pronounced tumor signal drop at ∼12 h post-injection, providing an imaging-defined irradiation window. RGD decoration improves cellular internalization (DiO-positive cells 80.6% vs . 55.8% at 3 h) and, together with NIR activation, increases ROS-associated signals, mitochondrial depolarization, and apoptosis (up to 46.4%) in vitro . In Hepa1-6 tumor-bearing mice, the image-guided combined regimen markedly suppresses tumor growth, reducing endpoint tumor weight from 1.1 g (PBS) to 0.1 g (91% reduction) without obvious acute toxicity under the tested conditions. This work establishes an operational "MRI-defined window → mild hyperthermia → thermosensitive release" paradigm to localize SRF action and improve the efficacy-toxicity balance for HCC therapy.

title: Clinical Spectrum and Insights from One Year of Ocular Genetics at a Single Tertiary Eye Care Centre.
abstract: Introduction Genetic testing benefits individuals and families with inherited eye diseases by facilitating accurate diagnosis, informing prognosis, enabling assessment for at-risk family members, and supporting targeted therapies. This study aimed to characterize the spectrum of inherited eye disorders and evaluate the diagnostic yield of genetic testing at a single tertiary eye care centre over a one-year period. Methods A retrospective review of patients attending the ocular genetics service at a tertiary eye care centre in India from January 1 to December 31, 2024, was conducted. Results Of 1325 patients evaluated, 862 (65%) underwent genetic testing. Inherited retinal disorders were the most common ( n = 440, 51%), followed by cornea and anterior segment disorders ( n = 107, 12.4%). Other conditions included hereditary optic nerve disorders ( n = 75, 8.7%), glaucoma ( n = 70, 8.1%), lenticular disorders ( n = 54, 6.3%), phacomatoses ( n = 25, 2.9%), ocular tumours ( n = 20, 2.3%), strabismus and albinism ( n = 19 and 18; ~2% each), MAC spectrum disorders ( n = 10, 1.4%), and systemic syndromes ( n = 22, 2.5%). Diagnostic yield was achieved in 605 (70%), while 257 (30%) remained inconclusive. Of the 463 untested families, the motivations were unascertained reasons ( n = 156, 33%), financial constraints ( n = 138, 30%), intent to test later ( n = 90, 19%), and belief that no treatment was available ( n = 79, 17%). Discussion Inherited retinal and anterior segment disorders constitute the most frequent genetic eye diseases. Genetic testing has enabled genotype-phenotype correlation in over two-thirds of cases. Financial constraints and limited availability of disease-modifying treatments remain key barriers for uptake of genetic testing.

Inherited retinal and anterior segment disorders constitute the most frequent genetic eye diseases. Genetic testing has enabled genotype-phenotype correlation in over two-thirds of cases. Financial constraints and limited availability of disease-modifying treatments remain key barriers for uptake of genetic testing.

title: Multimodal Imaging Characteristics of Sarcoid Retinal Granulomas.
abstract: Purpose To describe the clinical presentation and multimodal imaging characteristics of retinal granulomas in patients with ocular sarcoidosis. Methods In this retrospective observational case series, patients with definite or presumed ocular sarcoidosis presenting with retinal granulomas were evaluated. Multimodal retinal imaging was reviewed to characterize lesion morphology, imaging patterns, and longitudinal evolution. Results Retinal granulomas were identified in three patients with ocular sarcoidosis from diverse racial backgrounds. On fundus photographs, lesions ranged from multiple, superficial, small, faint yellow-gray nodules to more distinct, deeper yellow lesions, predominantly located in the mid- to peripheral retina. All retinal granulomas demonstrated hyperreflectivity on OCT with four distinct morphologic patterns: (1) inner and/or outer retinal granulomas; (2) retinal granulomas associated with retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) disruption and hypertransmission defects; (3) sub-RPE granulomas located between the RPE and Bruch's membrane; and (4) combined chorioretinal granulomas extending from the choroid. FAF demonstrated predominantly isoautofluorescent lesions in the absence of RPE involvement, whereas hypoautofluorescence was observed when the RPE was involved. FA was available for one patient and demonstrated late hyperfluorescent staining of the retinal granulomas. Longitudinal imaging demonstrated evolution from active inflammatory nodules to regression with residual retinal and/or RPE changes, commonly manifesting as punched-out atrophic lesions. Conclusion Retinal granulomas may represent an underrecognized manifestation of ocular sarcoidosis. In our series, multimodal imaging allowed detailed characterization of their morphologic patterns and longitudinal evolution. Recognition of these characteristic imaging features of sarcoid retinal granulomas may facilitate consideration of sarcoidosis in the differential diagnosis of retinal infiltrative lesions.

title: Post-treatment risks of transcatheter aortic valve implantation: should we be increasing preventative measures?
abstract: Introduction Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has become an established treatment for severe aortic stenosis across an expanding risk spectrum. As indications extend to younger and lower-risk patients, post-treatment complications with implications for survival, quality of life, and valve durability require attention. Areas covered This narrative review discusses major post-TAVI complications with direct implications for procedural planning and lifetime management, including cerebrovascular events, conduction abnormalities, coronary obstruction and aortic root injury, bioprosthetic valve dysfunction, valve thrombosis, residual regurgitation, and TAVI-associated infective endocarditis. Evidence was reviewed from pivotal randomized trials, contemporary registries, consensus documents, systematic reviews, and mechanistic studies addressing incidence, pathophysiology, predictors, prognosis, prevention, diagnosis, and management of these complications. Expert opinion Post-TAVI risk reduction should move beyond reactive complication management toward individualized prevention. Meticulous computed tomography-based planning, optimized valve selection and implantation technique, rational antithrombotic therapy, structured rhythm and valve surveillance, selective use of cerebral embolic protection, timely correction of clinically or hemodynamically significant residual regurgitation, and infection-prevention pathways are central components of contemporary care. Future progress will depend on better risk stratification, longer-term durability data, and targeted preventive strategies adapted to lower-risk patients with longer life expectancy.

title: Towards artificial intelligence based preoperative dosimetry for liver<sup>90</sup>Y selective internal radiation therapy.
abstract: Objective. Selective internal radiation therapy delivers Y-90 microspheres through the hepatic arterial system to achieve tumoricidal absorbed dose while limiting normal-tissue irradiation. Current pre-treatment dosimetry requires angiography and 99 mTc-MAA imaging, resulting in an invasive and resource-intensive workflow. This study evaluates the feasibility of estimating post-therapy Y-90 dose distribution directly from diagnostic multiphasic CT using an automated deep-learning pipeline, without requiring angiography or surrogate-particle imaging. Approach. In 152 treatments from the multicenter PROACTIF registry, arterial- and portal-phase CT, together with clinically documented perfusion territories and injected activities, were processed through automated segmentation, rigid registration, differential CT generation, and a generative model synthesizing a PET-like Y-90 activity map. Absorbed-dose maps were computed using the Local Dose Deposition method, and predictive accuracy was assessed using tumor dose-volume metrics and voxelwise spatial agreement. Main results. For the best-performing configuration, the median tumor D70 error was 23 Gy, with substantial inter-patient variability reflecting the challenges of CT-only dose prediction. High-dose coverage (V200) showed a similar pattern. In contrast, spatial agreement was consistently strong, with perfused-volume gamma passing rates around 93% and tumor-level rates around 85%, indicating that the macro-scale distribution of microspheres can be approximated from diagnostic CT. The full pipeline was fully automated and produced predictive dosimetry in under 30 S. Significance. Pre-angiography CT contains exploitable information about arterial enhancement and perfusion patterns that enables feasible CT-only prediction of Y-90 spatial distribution. While tumor-level absorbed-dose metrics remain variable, the strong spatial agreement suggests potential utility as an early planning tool to support patient selection or guide catheterization strategy prior to angiography.

title: Impact of depth-of-interaction and spatially-variant point-spread-function model on the performance of ultra-high resolution brain PET.
abstract: Objective. To implement a spatially-variant point spread function (VarPSF) model for the NeuroEXPLORER (NX) brain positron emission tomography (PET) scanner in the open-source Yale Reconstruction Toolkit for PET, and investigate the interplay between depth-of-interaction (DOI) resolution and resolution modeling. Approach. PSF parameters were estimated from simulated and physically measured point sources. Three primary DOI configurations were evaluated: eight-layer DOI (8DOI), two-layer DOI (2DOI), and no DOI (noDOI), with an additional 4DOI comparison in the off-center simulated Derenzo study. Reconstructions using VarPSF, a spatially-invariant PSF measured at the field-of-view center (SinglePSF), and no PSF modeling (noPSF) were assessed using simulated Derenzo and brain phantoms, a physical Derenzo phantom, and one non-human primate (NHP) scan. Main results. In simulated and physical Derenzo studies, VarPSF yielded higher peak-to-valley ratios than SinglePSF and noPSF at the final evaluated iterations, with pronounced gains at large radial offsets. In the simulated brain phantom, VarPSF reduced the estimated transverse blur by 0.3 mm relative to SinglePSF and 0.5 mm relative to noPSF in 2DOI, and by 0.6 mm and 0.8 mm, respectively, in noDOI. In the NHP study, VarPSF improved contrast and structural delineation with reduced DOI encoding at approximately matched white-matter coefficient of variation, while its incremental benefit over SinglePSF was small with 8DOI at clinically relevant iteration settings. Significance. Spatially-variant PSF modeling can partially compensate for limited DOI information. The findings motivate combining modest DOI capability with accurate resolution modeling, while further validation is required for redesigned detectors and fully corrected acquisitions. The open-source implementation enables controlled investigation of the complementary roles of DOI encoding and resolution modeling.

title: A wavelet-guided diffusion method for brain magnetic resonance parameter mapping using MOLED-based datasets: proof-of-principle.
abstract: Objective. Quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (qMRI) can noninvasively acquire parametric maps, providing quantitative biomarkers for clinical assessment. Parametric maps, such as T 2 , T 2 * , and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), characterize distinct biophysical processes in tissue in an interpretable, numerical manner. Owing to their distinct physical origins, various parametric maps differ in physical units, numerical magnitudes, and dynamic ranges. Even for the same type of parametric map, inter-subject differences may still exist in anatomical morphology, tissue characteristics, and the local distributions of parameter values. However, deep learning methods trained in image-domain directly learn pixel-level parameter values, and variations in numerical scales and subject-specific parameter distributions may result in anatomical detail loss and localized artifacts in certain tasks. To address this challenge and to deliver dependable quantitative references for clinical assessment, we propose a wavelet-guided diffusion method. Approach. We extend the discrete convolution wavelet transform (DCWT) to two dimensions and combine it with a conditional denoising diffusion method to develop a diffusion-based DCWT (Diff-DCWT) for parameter mapping. Diff-DCWT achieves accurate parameter mapping under the guidance of wavelet coefficient maps, thereby reducing reliance on image domain learning. The performance of Diff-DCWT is evaluated through simulation and in vivo experiments across T 2 , T 2 * , and ADC mapping tasks. Main Results. Both simulation and healthy volunteer experiments demonstrate that T 2 , T 2 * , and ADC maps obtained from Diff-DCWT maintain excellent visual quality and quantitative accuracy. Clinical case studies suggest the potential utility of Diff-DCWT-derived T 2 and ADC maps for stroke staging and help distinguish lesional from normal brain regions in glioma. Significance. Diff-DCWT establishes a high-fidelity framework for parameter mapping and exhibits preliminary clinical value in stroke staging and glioma characterization. Moreover, this work demonstrates the potential of wavelet-domain prior guidance for deep learning-based qMRI applications.

title: High-fidelity 3D geometric reconstruction of pelvic organs from MRI: a hybrid deep learning and iterative optimization approach.
abstract: Objective The generation of high-fidelity, high-quality three-dimensional (3D) pelvic organ geometries from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived segmentation masks remains challenging. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a hybrid framework for reconstructing the bladder, uterus, and rectum, and to assess its geometric fidelity, mesh-quality proxy performance, and reconstruction efficiency. Approach. We developed a hybrid deformable shape modeling framework that integrates deep learning prediction with iterative optimization for the reconstruction of the bladder, uterus, and rectum. The framework consists of three core components: (1) a geometry-aware multi-level deep learning architecture that preserves topological consistency of pelvic organs; (2) a two-stage amortized optimization training strategy that balances global shape capture and local surface refinement; and (3) a holistic synergy mechanism-where iterative optimization provides supervision for deep learning during the training phase, and during inference, deep learning rapidly predicts the global organ morphology, followed by iterative optimization to refine local surfaces and mesh quality. Main results. Before iterative refinement, the proposed model outperformed representative deep learning-based reconstruction methods in geometric fidelity, achieving CD/DSC values of 5.5 × 10⁻³/0.788 for the bladder, 3.7 × 10⁻³/0.839 for the rectum, and 4.2 × 10⁻³/0.900 for the uterus. Deep learning-based initialization enabled the complete hybrid framework to converge within approximately 100 iterations, with a reconstruction time of approximately 35 s per organ on a CPU and 1.5 s on a GPU. At the patient level, the mean minSICN and minSIGE values of the 10 worst volumetric elements were 0.0807 and 0.0844, respectively, exceeding those achieved by traditional geometric post-processing methods. Significance. The proposed framework connects image-domain segmentation with structural-domain applications by efficiently generating high-fidelity, high-quality pelvic organ geometries with improved mesh-quality proxy performance. These geometries may support statistical shape assessment and may provide candidate surface representations for subsequent volumetric meshing and solver-specific biomechanical validation.

title: Adaptive physics-inspired angular-spatial modeling for multi-shell diffusion MRI denoising.
abstract: Objective Multi-shell diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) provides rich q-space information but is susceptible to noise, which can disrupt spatial anatomy, intra-shell directional relationships, inter-shell signal attenuation, and downstream diffusion parameter estimation. We aim to develop a denoising method that jointly preserves spatial structure, directional information, and shell-specific signal characteristics. Approach We propose ASD-NCSM, an adaptive physics-inspired angular-spatial framework with a fixed three-stage alternating architecture. It combines intra-shell differential angular graph message passing with 2.5D spatial residual refinement. Noise-Conditioned Shell Modulation (NCSM) adaptively regulates angular updates according to b-value, spatial residual and angular dispersion proxies, and local gating. A Shell-wise Physical Attenuation and Angular Relation Consistency (SPARC) objective further constrains shell-wise signal fidelity, logarithmic attenuation, and local angular structure. The model was evaluated on HCP multi-shell dMRI with simulated noise and independently acquired real in vivo brain dMRI data. Main results Across five simulated noise levels from 2% to 10%, ASD-NCSM achieved the best overall DWI restoration among MPPCA, 1D-CNN, ECDM, SAN2N, and dMRI-Swin, with consistent subject-level advantages in PSNR, SSIM, and NRMSE. At 6% noise, principal-direction angular nRMSE was 32.68 ± 2.76%, with significant differences from all five baselines after Holm correction. ASD-NCSM also achieved the lowest mean MAE for FA, MD, AD, and RD, and the lowest relative MAE for ODI and FISO, while NDI was comparable to 1D-CNN and dMRI-Swin. For real data without noise-free references, Q-PEFT yielded the lowest angular cross-fit inconsistency (2.29 ± 0.10%) across three test subjects while maintaining limited signal and downstream-parameter changes. Significance ASD-NCSM jointly preserves spatial continuity, directional geometry, and shell-level attenuation, providing balanced signal recovery, directional preservation, and downstream parameter stability for multi-shell dMRI denoising.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
abstract: Objective Limited-angle cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is attractive for imageguided radiotherapy and imaging-guided procedure when full-arc acquisition is impractical, but the incomplete angular sampling leads to severe streaking, shading, and structural distortion. This study aimed to develop a physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction framework for recovering anatomically faithful volumetric CBCT from limited-angle projections. Approach: We propose PCGA-Net, a dual-domain reconstruction framework that combines projection completion, analytic geometric reconstruction, and image-domain refinement within a unified cross-domain design. Specifically, a projection completion module first estimates missingangle information from the measured limited-angle projections. A geometry-aware reconstruction module then maps the completed projections into image space using differentiable cone-beam forward and backward-projection operators. Finally, a volumetric refinement module suppresses residual artifacts and restores anatomical detail under geometry-guided cross-domain consistency supervision. The framework was evaluated on three cohorts: gynecologic highdose-rate brachytherapy, abdominal liver 4DCT, and head-and-neck CBCT. Main Results: Across all three cohorts, PCGA-Net consistently outperformed conventional limitedangle FDK reconstruction and the compared learning-based baselines, cGAN and PatRecon-Net, in both qualitative and quantitative evaluation. On the gynecologic HDR brachytherapy cohort, PCGA-Net achieved an MAE of 34.47 ± 6.28 HU, an SSIM of 0.87 ± 0.04, and a PSNR of 35.79 ± 0.95 dB. On the abdominal liver 4DCT cohort, PCGA-Net achieved 39.27 ± 6.10 HU MAE, 0.82 ± 0.03 SSIM, and 36.85 ± 1.16 dB PSNR.On the head-and-neck CBCT cohort, PCGA-Net achieved 28.42 ± 4.88 HU MAE, 0.91 ± 0.05 SSIM, and 38.52 ± 0.95 dB PSNR. In all three cohorts, PCGA-Net exceeded cGAN and PatRecon-Net across all evaluated metrics. Significance: These results indicate that jointly enforcing projection-domain completion, analytic imaging geometry, and image-domain refinement is an effective strategy for limited-angle CBCT reconstruction. PCGA-Net provides a robust short-arc reconstruction framework across multiple anatomical sites, supporting its potential utility in constrained imageguided therapeutic and procedural settings.

title: Patient-specific dosimetric impact of online adaptive radiotherapy for locally advanced cervical cancer.
abstract: Background: When cervical cancer patients are treated with external beam radiation therapy, patient-specific anatomical changes, particularly bladder filling, alter the position and shape of the target volume throughout treatment. Online adaptive radiotherapy (oART) accounts for these interfractional changes by generating a treatment plan based on the patient's daily anatomy. Purpose: This study evaluated the dosimetric impact of oART and investigated the relationship between patient-specific anatomical changes and the dosimetric of benefit of adaptation using standard cone-beam CT (CBCT) images for locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC). Methods: Ten patients previously treated for LACC at our institution were identified. A reference treatment plan incorporating a 5 mm clinical target volume (CTV)-to-planning target volume (PTV) margin was generated within the planning system simulator. Three CBCT images (Fractions 1, 13, and 25) were used to retrospectively simulate an adaptive treatment session. For each CBCT, the reference plan was recalculated on the daily anatomy to generate a scheduled plan, and an adapted plan was generated for comparison based on target coverage and organ at risk (OAR) dose metrics. The relationship between interfraction anatomical variation and the dosimetric benefit of adaptation was evaluated. Results: Adapted plans improved target coverage while generally maintaining or reducing OAR dose relative to the scheduled plans. However, the magnitude of benefit from adaptation varied between patients. Moderate associations were observed between interfraction anatomical variation of the bladder volume change and improvements in target coverage. Conclusion: The dosimetric benefit of oART was patient-specific and was partially associated with interfraction anatomical variation. These findings support an individualized approach to identify patient-specific characteristics that may help determine what patients would benefit the most from adaptive radiotherapy.

title: A multi-atlas ensemble learning framework for autism spectrum disorder diagnosis.
abstract: Objective. Clinical autism spectrum disorder (ASD) relies on subjective scales and neuroimaging, with traditional approaches suffering from high subjectivity and insufficient feature extraction, increasing misdiagnoses risk. Approach. To improve the diagnostic accuracy, we propose a multimodal ASD prediction network (APN) that integrates resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging with non-imaging data. Algorithmically, we first introduce a novel cumulative distribution divergence score (CDDS) feature selection method based on the multi-atlas functional connectivity (FC), which quantifies statistical distributional differences between positive and negative samples, effectively addressing the limitations of the traditional F -score in overlapping or weakly discriminative features. Building upon this, we adapt existing deep learning (DL) paradigms to construct a deep neural architecture (variational autoencoder-denoising autoencoder (VAEA)), combining a variational autoencoder (VAE), a denoising autoencoder, and a multilayer perceptron. The combination of these modules is non-trivial: the novel CDDS first purifies the high-dimensional feature space, enabling the VAEA to learn robust latent probabilistic representations via unsupervised pre-training without suffering from the curse of dimensionality. This is followed by the supervised fine-tuning to optimize parameters. We further incorporate demographic factors including age, full-scale intelligence quotient, and gender via a late-fusion strategy to prevent them from being overshadowed by imaging features, thereby enhancing the discriminability. FC features from three atlases including AAL, CC400, and Dosenbach160 are weighted and integrated to achieve the effective multi-source fusion. Main results. We conduct 10-fold cross-validations on the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) dataset, and the proposed APN achieves 81.63% accuracy, 81.89% sensitivity and 81.46% specificity, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Interpretability analysis identifies hippocampus, amygdala, and cingulate gyrus as strongly ASD-associated regions, offering neural mechanistic insights. Significance. This study provides an efficient, objective, and interpretable multimodal DL framework for ASD assisted diagnosis, with substantial clinical application and neuroscience value.

title: Wavelet-based adaptive image fusion of CT and MRI with local neighborhood variance for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
abstract: Multimodal imaging of nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) requires complementary representation of CT-derived bony anatomy and MRI-derived soft-tissue contrast. Existing fusion methods may fail to preserve both structural detail and soft-tissue information in a transparent and reproducible manner. We present a wavelet-based fusion framework that employs local neighborhood variance for adaptive weighting. This interpretable variance-driven strategy selectively integrates CT bony structures and MRI soft-tissue textures according to regional information content. The neighborhood configuration was selected through an ablation analysis of 232 clinical cases. Quantitative evaluation showed improved image-quality performance over the selected comparison methods across entropy, spatial frequency, average gradient, standard deviation, and edge information preservation factor, with respective gains of approximately 5.5%, 2.4%, 6.7%, 5.1%, and 3.2% relative to the best-performing baseline for each metric. These findings support the proposed method as an image fusion methodology for preserving complementary multimodal information; direct effects on target delineation, workflow efficiency, or dosimetric outcomes require future clinical validation.

title: Breast Implant Flipping: Prevalence, Clinical Correlation, and Independent Risk Factors in a Consecutive Ultrasound Cohort.
abstract: Background Silicone breast implants are designed with an anterior domed surface, and relatively flat posterior surface that contains the cured silicone patch. With implant flipping (an anterior-posterior malposition), the posterior patch rotates to an anterior position. Objectives There are currently no prospective published studies reporting the prevalence of implant flipping and its associated symptoms in aesthetic patients. This prospective study used in-office high-resolution ultrasound (HRUS) to evaluate the prevalence of breast implant flipping, assess associated changes in breast shape, appearance, and symptoms, and identify potential risk factors. Methods Consecutive patients with silicone breast implants presenting for routine follow-up underwent HRUS at 7 study sites in the United States over a 4-month period between April 1st and August 1st, 2026. Demographic data included age and BMI. Implant data included time since surgery, whether a primary of revision procedure, number of revisions, manufacturer, size, style, surface, use of ADM or scaffold, pocket location, capsule grade, flipped or not, and rupture. Results Five hundred and ninety consecutive patients were enrolled over 4 months. Mean age 43 years with range 22-82, mean BMI 23 with range of 16-34.5. Primary augmentations accounted for 64.6% of procedures, while revision augmentations accounted for 35.4%. Device manufacturer distribution, 63.9% Allergan, 12.4% Mentor, 15.9% Motiva, and 7.1% Sientra. Implant flipping was identified in 75 patients (12.7%). Conclusions Implant flipping was identified by HRUS in one in eight patients. Larger implant volume, prepectoral placement, and lack of soft tissue support were independently associated with flipping. HRUS improves detection, patient counseling, and surgical planning.

title: Modern Radiotherapy for Axial Giant Cell Tumor of Bone: Impact of Gross Disease at Treatment Initiation.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate outcomes of modern radiotherapy (RT) for giant cell tumor of bone (GCTB) in anatomically constrained axial sites and to assess the prognostic impact of disease burden at RT initiation. Methods We retrospectively reviewed consecutive patients with pathologically confirmed GCTB of the spine, sacrum, or skull treated with RT between 2006 and 2024 at a single institution. Patients treated with palliative intent and 1 patient lost to follow-up immediately after RT were excluded. Local recurrence-free survival (LRFS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were calculated from RT initiation. Gross disease at RT was defined as a radiographically visible lesion on CT and/or MRI at RT initiation. Survival was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared by the log-rank test; prognostic factors were explored using univariate analyses. Results Seventeen patients were included (postoperative RT, n=13; salvage RT, n=3; definitive RT, n=1) and treated with 3D-conformal RT (n=9), IMRT (n=3), or proton therapy (n=5). Median follow-up was 79.8 months. The 5-year LRFS and PFS rates were 75.1% and 68.3%, respectively. Four patients experienced local recurrence and 1 developed lung metastasis. Gross disease at RT initiation (n=8) was significantly associated with inferior LRFS (5 y LRFS: 46.9% vs. 100.0% without gross disease; P=0.018). Conclusions In this cohort of axial GCTB treated with modern RT, gross disease at RT initiation was associated with inferior local control. Outcomes appeared more favorable when RT was delivered in the absence of gross disease, suggesting that maximal safe debulking before RT may be relevant in selected anatomically constrained cases.

title: Anterior Segment Ischemia and Neurotrophic Keratopathy Following Ultrasound Cycloplasty in Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma.
abstract: Ultrasound cycloplasty (UCP) is a minimally invasive, non-incisional glaucoma procedure that has emerged in recent years and is generally associated with few complications. We report a case of a patient with acute angle-closure glaucoma underwent UCP for IOP control. She developed iris neovascularization and neurotrophic keratopathy（NK）at postoperative week 6, followed by hypopyon, flattening of the anterior chamber, and thinning of the peripheral cornea at postoperative week 11, 12, and 14, respectively. We concluded that UCP can lead to anterior segment ischemia (ASI) and NK, which manifest as iris neovascularization, painless corneal epithelial defects, peripheral corneal thinning, hypopyon, and flattening of the anterior chamber. Preoperative screening for high-risk factors is essential before performing UCP.

title: What is the Utility of Whole Body Imaging for Screening Patients With Craniofacial Fibrous Dysplasia?
abstract: Whole body imaging is commonly performed in patients with fibrous dysplasia (FD) to screen for additional lesions. However, the frequency of newly-detected lesions in patients presenting with isolated craniofacial FD is unclear. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the frequency of newly-detected FD lesions on whole body imaging in patients with craniofacial FD and no known extracraniofacial lesions or symptoms. This was a retrospective observational cohort study at a tertiary children's hospital in an urban setting. The study population consisted of patients with craniofacial FD who underwent whole body imaging with technetium-99m (Tc-99m) bone scintigraphy or fluorine-18 sodium fluoride positron emission tomography/computed tomography (F-18 NaF PET/CT). Patients with previously identified extracraniofacial lesions, symptoms, or McCune-Albright syndrome were excluded. The primary outcome was the frequency of newly-detected extracraniofacial FD lesions. Fifteen subjects were included (80% female). Mean age at FD diagnosis was 9.6±4.3 years, and mean age at imaging was 10.4±4.2 years. Tc-99m bone scintigraphy was the most common imaging modality (86.7%). Newly-detected extracraniofacial FD lesions were observed in 1 of 15 subjects (6.7%). Two additional subjects (13.3%) had incidental skeletal findings related to recent traumatic injuries. In patients presumed to have isolated craniofacial FD, whole body imaging identified a low frequency of extracraniofacial skeletal lesions. These findings suggest that routine screening may be considered selectively based on clinical history and physical examination. Further investigation is required to develop evidence-based screening guidelines.

title: In older adults, "mild" by GCS does not mean low risk: Multicenter study of 1,157 patients with mild TBI and acute subdural hematoma.
abstract: Background Acute traumatic subdural hematoma (SDH) is the most common intracranial injury in mild TBI (mTBI), particularly in older adults. However, the relationship of patient and brain computed tomography (CT) characteristics with outcomes remains poorly described in a contemporary cohort. This study aims to characterize outcomes in younger and older adults with mTBI and isolated acute SDH. Methods This was a 10-center, retrospective cohort study of adult traumas with emergency department Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) 13 to 15 and acute traumatic SDH on initial brain CT ('22-'23). Trauma registry, EHR, and Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS) data were collected through automated and manual methods. The primary outcome was total mortality (TM=death+hospice discharge); the sample was stratified by 18 to 64 versus older than or equal to 65 years. Multivariable backward selection logistic regression examined 21 demographic, injury, and brain CT covariates. Results In total, 1,157 patients were included (18-64 y: 28%; ≥65 y: 72%; 58% transferred in). Median [IQR] non-head ISS was 1 [1-5] in 18 to 64 years, and 1 [1-2] in older than or equal to 65 years. Ten percent had neurosurgical intervention (18-64 y: 8%; ≥65 y: 11%). TM was higher in older than or equal to 65 years than 18 to 64 years (10% vs. 3%). Compared with older than or equal to 65 years, 18 to 64 years were discharged home more frequently (78% vs. 51%) and to hospice less frequently (2% vs. 7%). In 18 to 64 years, factors associated with TM were race, advance directive, functional dependence, ISS, more midline shift, and thicker SDH (too few TMs for adjusted models). In older than or equal to 65 years, factors independently associated with TM were advance directive (aOR [95% CI]: 11.8 [2.9-49.0]), male sex (3.0 [1.3-7.0]), midline shift (1.8 [1.3-2.6]), shock index (1.5 [1.1-2.1]), and worsening SDH on follow-up CT (2.9 [1.3-6.6]). Conclusions Despite presenting as "mild", these data highlight that older adults with SDH have high TM and should continue to receive the highest-level care with timely goals-of-care discussions. The association between advance directives and TM should be interpreted within the context of baseline vulnerability and preinjury treatment preferences, not as a biological mortality predictor. Level of evidence Level III, prognostic/epidemiological.

title: Noise2Match: Self-Supervised Low-Dose CT Denoising via Adaptive Inter-Slice Matching.
abstract: With the rapid development of deep learning, supervised convolutional neural network methods have greatly improved the performance of low-dose computed tomography (CT) denoising. However, they require paired noisy-clean training data, which is difficult to obtain in practice. Some classic self-supervised denoising methods rely on the assumption of pixel-wise independent noise, making them ineffective for correlated noise in low-dose CT (LDCT) images. Considering the high similarity and weaker noise correlation between adjacent CT slices, several recently proposed self-supervised methods use adjacent LDCT slices for training. Nevertheless, these approaches fail to effectively account for the non-rigid mis-alignment between slices caused by anatomical variation, hindering them from satisfying the equal-mean condition required by the classic Noise2Noise framework. In this paper, we propose Noise2Match, a self-supervised LDCT denoising method based on adaptive inter-slice matching. Noise2Match introduces an inter-slice matching network to model the label transition process between adjacent slices, and then applies correction to the denoiser's outputs to better satisfy the equal-mean condition. We theoretically prove that, under idealized conditions, training Noise2Match using adjacent LDCT slices is equivalent to supervised training with paired noisy-clean images. We further find that Noise2Match can also effectively perform low-dose cone-beam CT (CBCT) denoising, which could be attributed to its correction operation that reduces inter-slice noise correlation. To the best of our knowledge, Noise2Match is the first effective image-domain self-supervised method for low-dose CBCT. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Noise2Match outperforms existing image-domain self-supervised methods, offering broader applicability and higher practical value.

title: Integrating Plain 2D Ultrasound and Clinical Data for Identification of At-Risk MASH: A Multicenter Proof of Concept Study.
abstract: Background Identifying people with at-risk metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is a major challenge. We aimed to use deep learning to develop a convolutional neural network (CNN) model to facilitate the detection of at-risk MASH. Methods A multi-center cohort study was conducted across five tertiary hospitals in Japan and China. Clinical data and conventional ultrasound images were retrospectively collected. Organ segmentation using YOLO version 11 with quality control was performed, followed by creation of an EfficientNet-B6 CNN regression model, with image-level predictions averaged per patient, to estimate FAST and AGILE 3+ risk categories. Model performance was assessed using agreement across clinically relevant rule-out and rule-in thresholds, R 2 , root mean squared error (RMSE), and area under the receiver operating curve (AUROC). Results The final dataset comprised 416 patients for training (7643 images), 139 for internal validation (2463 images), and 154 for external testing (3539 images). The CNN model demonstrated good agreement with FAST (R 2 = 0.684; RMSE = 0.131; category agreement = 0.71) and moderate agreement with AGILE 3+ (R 2 = 0.445; RMSE = 0.1964; category agreement = 0.63). For FAST, AUROC was 0.974 (95% CI 0.947-0.993) for 0.35 and 0.932 (95% CI 0.884-0.969) for the 0.67 cut-off. For AGILE 3+, AUROC was 0.908 (95% CI 0.854-0.950) for 0.451 and 0.902 (95% CI 0.839-0.953) for the 0.679 cut-off. Conclusion The CNN model applied to clinical ultrasound images can approximate the accuracy of VCTE-based composite risk scores for detecting at-risk MASH. This may support the detection of at-risk MASH in settings with limited access to transient elastography.

title: Comparison Between Interlaminar and Transforaminal Endoscopic Lumbar Discectomy for Sciatic Scoliosis Secondary to Lumbar Disc Herniation: A Retrospective Study With a Minimum 1 Year Follow-Up.
abstract: Objective This study aims to compare the clinical and radiographic outcomes of interlaminar and transforaminal endoscopic lumbar discectomy (IELD and TELD) in the treatment of lumbar disc herniation (LDH) with sciatic scoliosis. Methods Patients with sciatic scoliosis secondary to LDH who had undergone IELD or TELD between January 2022 to June 2024 were reviewed. Radiographic parameters, including Cobb angle, apical vertebral translation (AVT), and coronal balance distance (CBD), were measured preoperatively and postoperatively to assess curve evolution. Clinical outcomes were evaluated using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) and the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI). Meanwhile, perioperative data were also collected. Comparisons between the groups were made by independent t-tests and χ 2 tests. Results A total of 134 patients in the IELD group and 103 patients in the TELD group were included in this study. There was no significant difference in intraoperative blood loss (13.4 ± 7.8 mL vs. 11.5 ± 7.1 mL, p = 0.067) and postoperative length of stay (2.5 ± 0.6 days vs. 2.5 ± 0.8 days, p = 0.378) between the two groups; however, the IELD group demonstrated shorter operation time (87.2 ± 17.4 min vs. 96.1 ± 23.3 min, p = 0.001) and fewer intraoperative fluoroscopy times (4.9 ± 0.7 vs. 10.3 ± 2.7, p < 0.001) compared to the TELD group. Both groups showed significant improvements in VAS and ODI scores (p < 0.05), with no significant differences between the groups. Before surgery, 86.9% (206/237) patients had a disc herniation at the convex side of the lumbosacral curve and 86.5% (205/237) patients showed a trunk shift toward the opposite side of disc herniation. After surgery, 91.8% (123/134) of the IELD group and 90.3% (93/103) of the TELD group achieved resolution of scoliosis (AVT ≤ 10 mm) within 12 months. At the final follow-up, the AVT, Cobb angle, CBD, and SVA in the IELD group were 2.7 ± 2.0 mm, 1.0° ± 0.8°, 1.2 ± 0.9 mm, and 3.4 ± 3.1 mm, respectively, with no significant differences compared to the 2.8 ± 2.7 mm, 1.1° ± 0.8°, 1.2 ± 0.8 mm, and 3.7 ± 3.5 mm in the TELD group. Conclusions Both IELD and TELD are effective and safe for LDH with sciatic scoliosis, with comparable radiographic and clinical outcomes in terms of scoliosis correction. IELD is associated with shorter operation time and fewer intraoperative fluoroscopy times in this cohort.
originalAbstract:
Objective

This study aims to compare the clinical and radiographic outcomes of interlaminar and transforaminal endoscopic lumbar discectomy (IELD and TELD) in the treatment of lumbar disc herniation (LDH) with sciatic scoliosis.

Methods

Patients with sciatic scoliosis secondary to LDH who had undergone IELD or TELD between January 2022 to June 2024 were reviewed. Radiographic parameters, including Cobb angle, apical vertebral translation (AVT), and coronal balance distance (CBD), were measured preoperatively and postoperatively to assess curve evolution. Clinical outcomes were evaluated using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) and the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI). Meanwhile, perioperative data were also collected. Comparisons between the groups were made by independent t-tests and χ2 tests.

Results

A total of 134 patients in the IELD group and 103 patients in the TELD group were included in this study. There was no significant difference in intraoperative blood loss (13.4 ± 7.8 mL vs. 11.5 ± 7.1 mL, p = 0.067) and postoperative length of stay (2.5 ± 0.6 days vs. 2.5 ± 0.8 days, p = 0.378) between the two groups; however, the IELD group demonstrated shorter operation time (87.2 ± 17.4 min vs. 96.1 ± 23.3 min, p = 0.001) and fewer intraoperative fluoroscopy times (4.9 ± 0.7 vs. 10.3 ± 2.7, p < 0.001) compared to the TELD group. Both groups showed significant improvements in VAS and ODI scores (p < 0.05), with no significant differences between the groups. Before surgery, 86.9% (206/237) patients had a disc herniation at the convex side of the lumbosacral curve and 86.5% (205/237) patients showed a trunk shift toward the opposite side of disc herniation. After surgery, 91.8% (123/134) of the IELD group and 90.3% (93/103) of the TELD group achieved resolution of scoliosis (AVT ≤ 10 mm) within 12 months. At the final follow-up, the AVT, Cobb angle, CBD, and SVA in the IELD group were 2.7 ± 2.0 mm, 1.0° ± 0.8°, 1.2 ± 0.9 mm, and 3.4 ± 3.1 mm, respectively, with no significant differences compared to the 2.8 ± 2.7 mm, 1.1° ± 0.8°, 1.2 ± 0.8 mm, and 3.7 ± 3.5 mm in the TELD group.

Conclusions

Both IELD and TELD are effective and safe for LDH with sciatic scoliosis, with comparable radiographic and clinical outcomes in terms of scoliosis correction. IELD is associated with shorter operation time and fewer intraoperative fluoroscopy times in this cohort.
